## 4. Revenue Model

### 4.1 Architecture of the engine

Revenue is built bottom-up in four stages — (1) visitor volume by day-type and season, (2) capacity and utilization from canonical fleet counts, (3) yield from the canonical price card, (4) attach and program revenue — and then reconciled three ways: monthly to Year 1's $1,280 K, annually to the five-year canon, and externally to Volume 2's independent market-side estimate (§7.3 there: ≈$860 K sessions, ≈$165 K F&B, ≈$100 K retail, ≈$75 K memberships, ≈$88 K corporate, ≈$88 K parties — each within rounding distance of the operating-side lines built here, which is the agreement you want from two models built from opposite ends).

### 4.2 Visitor volume by day-type and season

Assumptions: 360 operating days; Year 1 opens March (M1); day-types calibrated to Volume 2's funnel output of ~110 visitors/operating-day average, with peak days 220–300 and midweek 40–60.

| Day-type | Days/yr | Avg paid visitors/day | Paid visits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Peak (weekends, public/school holidays) | 118 | 195 | 23,010 |
| Midweek standard | 190 | 55 | 10,450 |
| Shoulder & event days (league nights, twilight events, corporate blocks) | 52 | 105 | 5,460 |
| **Total individual paid visits** | **360** | **108 avg** | **38,920** |

Check: 118×195 = 23,010; 190×55 = 10,450; 52×105 = 5,460; sum = **38,920** (÷360 = 108/day ✓ Volume 2). Member visits, party guests, and corporate attendees add ≈3,100 gate visits → **≈42,000 total visits**. Blended on-site spend = (1,280 − 6 sponsorship − 14 education) ÷ 42.0 = **$30.0/visitor**, inside Volume 2's $26–32 benchmark band.

### 4.3 Capacity and utilization from fleet counts

Assumptions: capacity is **concurrent operating stations**, not fleet size (cars queue for customers, not customers for cars — Volume 3, Chapter 2 doctrine); 2 Shift-slots per station-hour (20-min Shift + turnaround inside a 25–30 min cycle); 8 average revenue hours across 360 days.

| Division | Concurrent stations | Basis (fleet canon) |
|---|---|---|
| Motorsport (Tracks A/B) | 22 | 64 cars; track slots bind: 8 touring + 6 drift (Track A), 8 off-road (Track B) — Volume 3 |
| Construction — Mining | 12 | 30 machines; 3–4 excavator stations (of 6) + circulating dump trucks + loaders — 1:3 ratio |
| Agriculture | 8 | 12 tractors, implement-limited |
| Crawler park (Track C) | 13 | 16 crawlers, trail-section-limited |
| Premium supervised (Kabolite showcase + premium crawler line) | 2 | Artisan-supervised |
| **Phase 1 total** | **57** | |

Annual slot capacity = 57 stations × 8 h × 2 slots/h × 360 d = **328,320 Shift-slots**. Year 1 consumes 57,720 blocks (§4.4) → **17.6% slot utilization** — deliberately low, leaving ~5× headroom so growth to Year 3–5 requires marketing and retention, not capex (the Volume 4 "option value" argument, park-wide).

### 4.4 Shift & session revenue — Year 1 build

Assumptions: canonical price card (Casual $15/$22; Operator $26/$38; Day Pass $59; Family bundle $89); premium share of casual volume ~14% (hydraulics, FPV-prep, big crawlers); operator-conversion ~25% of session buyers; blocks per product as shown. Volumes follow from §4.2 visits × observed products-per-visit (~0.9 sessions/visit for individual visitors, the rest arriving inside passes/bundles/groups).

| Product | Unit price $ | Units sold | Revenue $K | Blocks consumed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Casual Shift — standard | 15 | 21,400 | 321.0 | 21,400 |
| Casual Shift — premium | 22 | 3,500 | 77.0 | 3,500 |
| Operator Shift — standard (2 blocks + pit stop) | 26 | 7,200 | 187.2 | 14,400 |
| Operator Shift — premium | 38 | 1,250 | 47.5 | 2,500 |
| Day Pass (avg 4 blocks used) | 59 | 1,440 | 85.0 | 5,760 |
| Family bundle (4 drivers × 2 shifts) | 89 | 770 | 68.5 | 6,160 |
| Member/party/corporate included blocks | in other lines | — | — | 4,000 |
| **Shift & session revenue / blocks** | | | **786.2** | **57,720** |

Checks: 321.0 + 77.0 + 187.2 + 47.5 + 85.0 + 68.5 = **786.2** ($84,960 and $68,530 shown rounded to 85.0/68.5). Blocks: 21,400 + 3,500 + 14,400 + 2,500 + 5,760 + 6,160 + 4,000 = **57,720** ✓ §4.3. Average yield = 786.2 ÷ 53.72 K revenue-bearing blocks = **$14.6/block** ($13.6/block across all blocks including bundled).

### 4.5 Membership MRR build

Assumptions: canonical tiers (Apprentice $29, Operator $59, Foreman $99); sales start Month 2; net adds accelerate with the license ladder and league seasons (Volume 9); churn 3.5%/month netted within the adds shown.

| Milestone | Apprentice | Operator | Foreman | Members | MRR $K |

| End Month 3 | 45 | 10 | 2 | 57 | 2.1 |
| End Month 6 | 105 | 30 | 7 | 142 | 5.5 |
| End Month 9 | 160 | 52 | 13 | 225 | 9.0 |
| End Month 12 | 240 | 82 | 22 | 344 | 14.0 |

Check (Month 12): 240×29 + 82×59 + 22×99 = 6,960 + 4,838 + 2,178 = $13,976 ≈ **$14.0 K MRR**. Year 1 recognized membership revenue (monthly curve in §4.8) = **$70 K**; exit run-rate $167 K/yr, which is why Year 2 membership revenue steps to $160 K. Year 3 assumes ~620 average members (mix 420/150/50 → $25.98 K MRR) → **≈$300 K** ✓ §4.9.

### 4.6 Corporate, parties, education

Assumptions: canonical anchors (corporate from $1,400 for 2 h/20 pax; parties from $349 for 10 children); demand pools per Volume 2 §7.2 step 5; averages exceed anchors because packages upsell (catering, extra Shifts, premium classes).

Assumptions: F&B kiosk-only in Phase 1 at **$3.76/gate visit** (42.0 K visits — 52% purchase incidence × $7.20 average ticket); retail counter at $2.00/visit; paid repair/upgrade services for customer-owned vehicles priced per Volume 7's service menu; sponsorship is deliberately token in Year 1 (two local partners) and grows with audience (Volume 9 sponsorship strategy).

Assumptions by year: **Y2** — frequency growth (leagues, licenses), membership base ×2.3, aviation soft-opens Month 23; **Y3** — first full year of the complete Phase 2 park (Aviation + Marine + restaurant: F&B steps up, per-cap rises); **Y4–Y5** — Phase 3 elements (indoor arena from Month ~44 removes weather ceiling; Academy scales education; night racing lifts peak yield). Growth sanity: Y2 exit run-rate (Months 23–24 at $186–204 K/month, §6.2) annualizes to ≈$2.3–2.4 M, making Y3's $2.6 M a ~10% step on Phase 2 completion — frequency and new divisions, not a larger catchment (consistent with Volume 2, §7.3).

Division attribution (Year 1, Shift + program revenue of $952 K): Motorsport ≈ $470 K, Construction & Agriculture ≈ $430 K, Crawler park & recovery ≈ $52 K — honouring both Volume 3's "highest single revenue engine" and Volume 4's "≈$410–470 K, roughly a third of park revenue" (430 ÷ 1,280 = 34%). Day-pass and bundle value is attributed by observed block consumption in RC WORLD OS.

> **Investor Note.** Three properties make this revenue model conservative rather than optimistic. First, **utilization is 17.6% of slot capacity in Year 1** and only ~24% by Year 3 — the park never needs to be busy in absolute terms to hit canon. Second, **recurring revenue compounds quietly**: memberships grow from 5% to 13% of revenue across five years, and every point of that mix shift stabilizes the winter months that drive break-even timing. Third, the model **excludes franchise income entirely** (royalties, fees, and the Volume 12 program are upside outside canon, pointed to in §10.3).

## 5. Operating Cost Model

### 5.1 Staffing plan & payroll

Assumptions: salaries are full-year costs in $K for a mid-size international city (adjust locally with the Volume 12 localization index); **on-costs 15%** (employer taxes, workers' compensation, basic benefits) applied to base; casual/seasonal flex staff cover peak days and are shown as a separate line; headcounts step with phases. Artisans are the customer-facing technician corps (canon).

**Year 1 establishment (18.5 FTE):**

| Role | FTE | Base $K each | Base $K total |
|---|---|---|---|
| General Manager | 1 | 70 | 70 |
| Operations Manager | 1 | 52 | 52 |
| Workshop Lead (Head Artisan) | 1 | 48 | 48 |
| Artisans (technicians) | 4 | 36 | 144 |
| Track Marshals | 5 | 26 | 130 |
| Front-of-house / bookings | 3.5 | 24 | 84 |
| F&B kiosk staff | 2 | 24 | 48 |
| Marketing & community | 1 | 38 | 38 |
| Admin / bookkeeper | 1 | 30 | 30 |
| **Base payroll** | **18.5** | | **644** |
| On-costs @ 15% | | | 97 |
| Casual peak flex + recruitment & training | | | 26 |
| **Year 1 people cost** | | | **767** |

Check: 70+52+48+144+130+84+48+38+30 = 644; 644 × 1.15 = 740.6 ≈ 741; 741 + 26 = **767**.

**Year 3 establishment (≈24.5 FTE + restaurant team):** GM 74; Ops Manager 56; Workshop Lead 52; Artisans 6 × 37 = 222; Marshals 6 × 26 = 156; Front-of-house 4 × 24 = 96; restaurant/F&B team 125; Marketing 48; Admin/finance 38 → base 867; × 1.15 = 997; + casual flex 43 = **1,040**. Headcount growth over five years tracks divisions, not overhead: the Year 5 additions are marshals for Aviation/Marine, restaurant staff, and two Artisans — management stays at three salaried leaders plus the GM.

| People cost ($K) | Y1 | Y2 | Y3 | Y4 | Y5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total people | 767 | 940 | 1,040 | 1,217 | 1,351 |
| As % of revenue | 59.9% | 49.3% | 40.0% | 40.2% | 39.7% |

The people ratio falling from 60% to 40% is the core of the margin story (§7.2): a safety-credible venue must be fully staffed on Day 1, so revenue growth outruns headcount growth.

### 5.2 Fleet maintenance, parts & batteries

Assumptions: Year 1 fleet duty = 57,720 blocks × 20 min = 19,240 vehicle-hours + ~760 staff/test/practice hours ≈ **20,000 vehicle-hours**. Parts cost per vehicle-hour is derived from the failure-rate table below (component MTBF from the Volume 7 failure library and Source-2 failure-point lists), then cross-checked top-down. Batteries are consumables: 450 packs, conservative 250-cycle service life at rental duty (spec 300–500), one pack-cycle per block.

| Component class (examples) | MTBF (veh-h) | Landed cost/event $ | Cost per veh-h $ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tires & wheels (knobby, drift slicks) | 60 | 14 | 0.23 |
| Suspension & steering (arms, knuckles, shock shafts, links) | 45 | 11 | 0.24 |
| Drivetrain (pinions, spurs, CVDs, diffs, bearings) | 55 | 16 | 0.29 |
| Servos (15/25 kg digital) | 220 | 24 | 0.11 |
| Motors & ESCs (540/550, brushless ESC events) | 400 | 52 | 0.13 |
| Bodies, mounts & cosmetic | 90 | 12 | 0.13 |
| Construction-specific (track pins, lead-screws, micro-switches) | 150 | 20 | 0.13 |
| Fasteners, lubricants, coating, misc consumables | — | — | 0.84 |
| **Blended parts cost per vehicle-hour** | | | **2.10** |

Check: 0.23+0.24+0.29+0.11+0.13+0.13+0.13+0.84 = **2.10** (motorsport runs ≈$2.60/h, construction ≈$1.30/h, crawlers ≈$1.10/h; the blend reflects the block mix). Battery math: 57,720 pack-cycles ÷ 250-cycle life = 231 packs/year × $23 = **$5.3 K** (budgeted $6 K including crash-damaged packs) — note each pack averages only 128 cycles/year (57,720 ÷ 450), so the *calendar* replacement horizon is ~2 years, matching the 2–3-year depreciation policy (§7.3).

| Fleet cost line ($K) | Y1 | Y2 | Y3 | Y4 | Y5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parts (veh-h × $/veh-h) | 42 | 64 | 78 | 92 | 104 |
| Batteries (cycle-life consumption) | 6 | 9 | 11 | 13 | 15 |
| Tires/consumables uplift & event wear | 10 | 15 | 18 | 22 | 25 |
| Tools, warranty freight, external services | 8 | 10 | 11 | 13 | 14 |
| **Fleet maintenance total** | **66** | **98** | **118** | **140** | **158** |

Check Y1: 42+6+10+8 = **66**. Maintenance cost per vehicle-hour (total basis) = 66,000 ÷ 20,000 = **$3.30/veh-h** — a headline KPI (§10.4). Fleet *renewal* (replacing worn-out vehicles) is sustaining **capex**, not opex: $36 K (Y1), $72 K, $150 K, $170 K, $190 K — rising with Phase 2/3 fleet size and utilization.

> **Investor Note.** The Year 1 EBITDA of −$100 K is a **feature of honest modelling, not a flaw of the business**: the park opens fully staffed and fully insured against a revenue base that takes 12–16 months to build its membership and corporate layers. The funding plan carries this loss explicitly (§3.1's $350 K operating-funding line). Beware any comparable plan showing positive EBITDA in the opening year of a staffed venue — it is usually understaffing safety roles or amortizing pre-opening costs into later years.

## 6. Cash Flow & Break-Even

### 6.1 Conventions of the monthly model

Opening cash = $750 K (the $2.6 M ask less $1,850 K Phase 1 capex, per §3.1 — all Phase 1 capex assumed spent by opening day). Sustaining fleet-renewal capex $3 K/month in Year 1 and $6 K/month in Year 2. Phase 2 capex spends $55 K/month in Months 13–18 and $75 K/month in Months 19–24 ($780 K in Year 2; the remaining $370 K falls in Months 25–30). The optional Phase 2 facility (§3.5) draws four $150 K tranches in Months 15, 17, 19, 21; interest at 0.75%/month (9% p.a.) on the drawn balance, paid monthly in arrears. Working-capital movements are treated as neutral (membership prepayments and gift-wallet float offset inventory growth; stated as a simplification). Tax: no cash tax in Years 1–2 (losses; §7.1).

Year 2: revenue 1,905 ✓, opex 1,751 ✓, EBITDA 154 ✓; facility draws 4 × 150 = 600 ✓; interest 1.1+1.1+2.2+2.2+3.4+3.4+4.5+4.5+4.5 = 26.9 ✓ (0.75% on the stepped balance). Every closing-cash cell = prior cell + net cash. Months 23–24 include the Aviation Division soft-opening (Month 23) adding ≈$25–35 K/month — the bridge to Year 3's full-park revenue.

### 6.3 Break-even — shown and explained

Monthly operating break-even = the month from which monthly EBITDA is positive **and stays positive**. Two arithmetic facts drive its timing. First, the steady Year-2 cost stack is ≈$118–125 K/month of effectively fixed cost (people, lease, insurance, software, base marketing) plus ≈17–19% of revenue in variable cost (COGS, fleet wear, payment fees, casual labor) — so break-even revenue ≈ 122 ÷ 0.82 ≈ **$149 K/month**. Second, the revenue ramp (membership MRR compounding, corporate pipeline maturing, league base load) crosses that line at **Month 16** ($156 K revenue vs $144 K opex = +$12 K) and never goes negative again in the base model (the shallowest subsequent month is Month 20 at +$2 K, the post-summer shoulder). The canonical band **Month 16–19** exists because the crossing month is sensitive to opening-date seasonality and ramp speed: an autumn opening, or a ramp 10% slower, slides the crossing to Months 18–19 without changing annual totals materially. (First *isolated* positive months occur earlier — Months 5–6 in the summer peak — but the plan does not call that break-even; sustained coverage of the winter trough is the test.)

### 6.4 Cumulative cash curve and minimum-buffer policy

The cash curve has three regimes visible in §6.2: a **shallow Year-1 glide** from $750 K to $614 K (the −$136 K Year-1 burn: −$100 K EBITDA − $36 K sustaining capex); a **Phase-2 construction trough** in early Year 2, bottoming at **$476 K in Month 14**, with the facility draws deliberately timed after the trough so equity cash never falls further; and a **self-funding climb** from Month 22 as monthly EBITDA outruns Phase 2 spend. Policy: **minimum cash ≥ $250 K at all times** — approximately three months of the survival-floor cost stack (§6.5) — with a board-notification trigger at $350 K. The base model's worst point ($476 K) holds a $226 K cushion above the floor; Chapter 9's downside scenarios are tested against exactly this policy.

### 6.5 The cost-flex ladder (downside machinery)

If revenue underperforms, costs flex in pre-agreed stages rather than ad-hoc cuts. The survival floor is the number Volume 2's sensitivity discussion references (≈$0.9 M/year): the minimum annualized cost stack that keeps the park open safely, ~$74 K/month.

| Stage (trigger) | Actions | Annualized stack $K |
|---|---|---|
| Plan (base) | Full Year-1 establishment | 1,380 |
| Flex 1 (revenue <85% of plan for 8 rolling weeks) | Freeze hiring; casual hours −30%; marketing remixed not cut; defer non-safety maintenance projects | ≈ 1,250 |
| Flex 2 (<75% for 8 weeks) | Midweek hours compressed; F&B menu simplified; sustaining capex paused; one FOH and one F&B role held vacant | ≈ 1,100 |
| Survival floor (<60%, board decision) | Skeleton crew 8 FTE (~420), lease 106 + minimum utilities/site 69, insurance 45, software 40, fleet safety-minimum 45, marketing 55, COGS at reduced volume ~90, admin 20 | **≈ 890 (the "$0.9 M line")** |

Check (floor): 420+106+69+45+40+45+55+90+20 = **890**. Even the survival floor keeps every safety-critical function (marshals within the 8 FTE, insurance, battery-room compliance) fully funded.

The short fleet life is honest economics, not conservatism: a rental car at Year-3 utilization genuinely is consumed in 2–3 years, and the sustaining-capex line (§5.2) is its cash twin.

### 7.4 Payback

Cumulative EBITDA runs −100 → 54 → 684 → 1,466 → 2,396 ($K) across Years 1–5 (each year adds §7.1's EBITDA row; e.g. 684 = −100 + 154 + 630). Against **Phase 1 invested capital ($1,850 K)**: the crossing occurs when 1,850 − 1,466 = 384 of Year 5's 930 has accrued → 384 ÷ 930 × 12 ≈ 5 months into Year 5 = **Month ~53, early Year 5**. Against **capital actually consumed** (the $2.6 M ask less the ~$221 K still held as cash at end-Year 5, §7.6 — i.e. $2,379 K): 2,379 − 1,466 = 913 ÷ 930 × 12 ≈ 12 months → **Month ~60, end of Year 5**. The ambitious scenario (§10.1) pulls Phase-1 payback to **Month ~44 (Year 4)**; the conservative case pushes it beyond Year 5. Hence the canonical statement: **full payback Year 4–5, base case** — Year 5 on the base numbers, Year 4 achievable on the upside case, with Phase 2/3 self-funded throughout so payback is never diluted by follow-on equity.

### 7.5 Investor returns — IRR / MOIC ranges

Assumptions: Structure A cap table (investor 65%, §3.4); exit at end of Year 5 (≈6 years from close, which precedes opening by ~12 months); exit value = EV/EBITDA multiple × Year-5 EBITDA + closing cash − debt (facility fully repaid by end-Year 5); LBE/FEC venue transactions historically clear 6–9× EBITDA for proven single sites (industry transaction ranges, 2024–2026) — 6.5×/7.5×/8.5× used. Franchise value (Volume 12) excluded.

| Scenario (Y5 EBITDA / closing cash) | 6.5× exit | 7.5× exit | 8.5× exit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conservative (520 / 100, no cash tax paid): equity value $K | 3,480 | 4,000 | 4,520 |
| — investor proceeds (65%) / MOIC / IRR | 2,262 / 0.87× / −2.3% | 2,600 / 1.00× / 0.0% | 2,938 / 1.13× / +2.1% |
| **Base (930 / 221): equity value $K** | **6,266** | **7,196** | **8,126** |
| — investor proceeds (65%) / MOIC / IRR | 4,073 / 1.57× / 7.8% | **4,677 / 1.80× / 10.3%** | 5,282 / 2.03× / 12.5% |
| Ambitious (1,280 / 560): equity value $K | 8,880 | 10,160 | 11,440 |
| — investor proceeds (65%) / MOIC / IRR | 5,772 / 2.22× / 14.2% | 6,604 / 2.54× / 16.8% | 7,436 / 2.86× / 19.1% |

Check (base/7.5×): 7.5 × 930 = 6,975 + 221 = 7,196; × 65% = 4,677; ÷ 2,600 = 1.80×; 1.80^(1/6) − 1 = 10.3%. Two upsides sit outside this table deliberately: **dividend capacity** of ~$300–400 K/year from Year 4 (post-facility-amortization free cash) adds ≈2–4 points of IRR if distributed rather than reinvested, and the **franchise program** (§10.3) is pure option value on the same equity.

> **Investor Note.** Read the base case honestly: **1.6–2.0× MOIC and high-single to low-double-digit IRR** is an infrastructure-flavored return, not a venture return — earned with real assets, a self-funding expansion path, capped follow-on exposure, and Year-4 dividend capacity. What makes the risk-reward attractive is the shape: the conservative case still returns ~0.9–1.1× (assets, cash, and a functioning business retain value), while the ambitious case and the franchise option carry venture-like upside. Investors seeking >20% IRR should price the franchise program into their thesis (Volume 12) or negotiate Structure B's downside seniority.

## 8. Pricing Strategy & Elasticity

### 8.1 How the canonical prices were set

The price card was benchmarked against the competitor set of Volume 2, Chapter 6, positioned on a simple rule: **price the Casual Shift below a karting heat and above a trampoline hour, because the experience sits between them in intensity and above both in novelty** — then let premium classes, time-extension, and bundles do the yield work.

| Benchmark (Volume 2, Ch 6) | Typical price | RC WORLD position |
|---|---|---|
| Karting, single heat (10–15 min) | $25–35 | Casual Shift $15 undercuts at 20 min — deliberate trial-friendly entry |
| Trampoline/adventure park, per hour | $15–25 | Operator Shift $26 ≈ 40+ min of operation + pit-stop theatre |
| VR venue, per session/hour | $30–60 | Premium Operator $38 with physical, photographable machines |
| RC rental venues (small format), 15–20 min | $10–20 | $15 at radically higher production value; $22 premium classes above the band |
| Dig This-class real-machinery experience | $170–330 | Premium construction Shifts deliver the fantasy at 1/14 scale for ~1/10 the price |
| Cinema family night (4 people) | $60–80 | Family bundle $89 for a two-hour active outing — the head-to-head the marketing plan targets |

### 8.2 Price ladders and bundle logic

Every step of the ladder is priced off the $15 base with a visible, defensible ratio — customers should *feel* the logic, and staff should be able to explain it in one sentence.

| Product | Price | Ratio logic (arithmetic) |
|---|---|---|
| Casual Shift — standard | $15 | Base unit: 1 block |
| Casual Shift — premium | $22 | 1.47× base: premium classes carry supervision and higher-value machines (hydraulics, FPV, big crawlers) |
| Operator Shift — standard | $26 | 2 blocks à la carte = $30; bundle saves $4 (13%) and includes the battery-swap pit stop — rewards commitment, smooths queues |
| Operator Shift — premium | $38 | 2 × $22 = $44 − $6 (14%) — same discount discipline |
| Day Pass | $59 | ≈ 5–6 casual blocks of value for 3.9× base; average redemption 4 blocks (§4.4) keeps per-block yield at $14.75 while capping the customer's spend anxiety |
| Family bundle | $89 | 4 drivers × 2 shifts = 8 blocks; à la carte $120; 26% family discount targets the highest-LTV segment |
| Memberships $29/$59/$99 | monthly | Priced at ≈2/4/6.6 casual blocks; pays back for the customer at 2–3 visits/month, exactly the frequency Volume 9's loyalty ladder engineers |
| Corporate from $1,400 | 2 h / 20 pax | = $70/head against a $90–150/head corporate-event market norm; catering and premium classes upsell to the $1,600 realized average (§4.6) |
| Parties from $349 | 10 children | = $34.90/child vs $25–45 party-market band; includes host, blocks, and party room |

### 8.3 Dynamic and peak pricing options

Phase 1 opens with **fixed prices** (trust-building and operational simplicity), with three instrumented options held ready in RC WORLD OS, activated only on evidence: (1) **peak/off-peak spread** — ±$3 on the Casual Shift (Sat-afternoon $18, midweek-morning $12), projected +4–6% Shift revenue at neutral volume based on observed FEC peak-pricing outcomes; (2) **Top-Up dynamic offers** — the existing T-5-minute top-up mechanic (canon) priced 10–20% below counter rate when the queue roster is empty, converting perishable slot inventory; (3) **event-yield pricing** — league entries and night events priced by demand tier. Elasticity beliefs used in Chapter 9 (category benchmarks, to be replaced by A/B evidence from Month 6): casual/family segments ≈ −0.8 around the $15 anchor; enthusiast/premium ≈ −0.4; corporate/parties ≈ −0.3.

### 8.4 Discount governance

Discounting is the fastest way to destroy a yield model, so it is governed: **headline prices never discount** (no "50% off Shifts" — it reprices the anchor permanently); all discounts flow through **defined channels with owners and caps** — schools/education 20% (owner: GM), corporate volume tiers to 15% (sales), member benefits as *included blocks* rather than % off (product design, Volume 9), promotional trials as time-boxed bundles (marketing, ≤500 units/quarter). Every comp and discount posts to a **comp register in RC WORLD OS** reviewed monthly against a ceiling of **2.5% of gross revenue**; Gears loyalty redemptions are budgeted separately at ≤1.5% of revenue as a marketing cost (Volume 9 mechanics).

> **Investor Note.** The pricing architecture is built so that **yield grows without headline price rises**: premium-class mix, operator conversion, day-pass redemption depth, membership penetration, and (later) peak spreads are five independent yield levers, each worth 2–6% of Shift revenue. The plan needs none of them heroically; Chapter 9 shows what ±15% on price itself would do, and §8.3's elasticity beliefs are why the model prefers mix to price.

## 9. Sensitivity Analysis

### 9.1 Method

Each stress is applied to the base model in isolation (ceteris paribus), then read out on the two management-critical outputs: **break-even month** (base: Month 16, band 16–19) and **Year 3 EBITDA** (base: $630 K, 24.2%). Flow-through logic: revenue-volume changes carry ≈82% contribution (variable costs ≈18% scale away); price changes carry ≈95% contribution net of payment fees, before elasticity feedback; volume-linked share of revenue ≈92% (memberships and sponsorship lag volume in-year).

### 9.2 Tornado table

| Scenario | Mechanics ($K arithmetic on Year 3) | Y3 EBITDA ($K / margin) | Break-even month |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Visitors +20%** | Rev +20% × 92% × 2,600 = +478; × 82% contribution → **+392** | 1,022 / 33% | ~Month 12–13 |
| **Visitors −20%** | Mirror: −478 revenue → **−392** | 238 / 11% | ~Month 24–28 |
| **Price +15%** (elasticity −0.4 enthusiast-weighted) | Price-bearing rev 2,360 × 15% = +354; volume gives back 2,360 × 6% × 82% ≈ −116 → **+238** | 868 / ~30% | ~Month 13–14 |
| **Price −15%** | Mirror with weaker volume recovery (families don't fully backfill): **−260** | 370 / ~16% | ~Month 20–23 |
| **Fleet maintenance +25%** | §5.2 Y3 line 118 × 25% = **−30** | 600 / 23.1% | +1 month (~17–20) |
| **Capex overrun +20%** (Phase 1 +$370) | No P&L effect; cash effect −370: opening cash 750 → 380; Month-14 trough 476 → 106, **breaching the $250 K floor** | 630 / 24.2% (unchanged) | Unchanged — but funding action required (§9.4) |
| **FX/shipping shock +30% on China sourcing** | Opex: parts+batteries+consumables ≈ 107 of Y3 fleet line × 30% ≈ **−32**/yr; capex: sustaining fleet 150 → ~195 (cash, not EBITDA) | 598 / 23.0% | +1 month (~17–20) |

Ordering confirms the tornado shape: **visitor volume (±$392 K) > price (±$238–260 K) > FX (−$32 K) ≈ maintenance (−$30 K)**, with capex overrun a *cash* risk rather than a P&L risk. This is why marketing spend is protected in the cost-flex ladder (§6.5) while maintenance over-run is absorbed: the model is demand-fragile and cost-robust — the right shape for a venue, and the reason the KPI dashboard (§10.4) leads with demand indicators.

### 9.3 Compound downside

The honest nightmare is correlated: −20% visitors *and* +25% maintenance *and* a capex overrun (a rushed build causing quality problems suppressing demand). Stacked: Year 3 EBITDA ≈ 630 − 392 − 30 ≈ $208 K (8%); break-even drifts to Months 26–30; the Month-14 cash trough breaches the floor. Survival mechanics: the cost-flex ladder holds the stack near Flex-2 (~$1.1 M) buying ≈$180 K/year back; Phase 2 defers per its gate (releasing the $780 K Year-2 spend and its facility); the $180 K unallocated reserve deploys. Modelled through, the park survives at roughly the conservative scenario of Chapter 10 with Phase 2 delayed 12 months — impaired returns (≈1× MOIC), not insolvency. That resilience is bought by three design choices: phase gating, the fixed-cost-light fleet, and the reserve inside the $2.6 M.

### 9.4 Downside triggers and mitigations

| Trigger (monitored in RC WORLD OS, monthly board pack) | Threshold | Pre-agreed mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Rolling 8-week revenue vs plan | <85% / <75% / <60% | Cost-flex Stages 1/2/floor (§6.5); marketing remix before any price action |
| Month-end cash vs policy floor | <$350 K notify / <$250 K act | Freeze sustaining capex; draw reserve; if pre-opening: descope ladder (§2.11) — theming → grandstand-class scope → never OS, safety, or spares |
| Capex committed vs budget (pre-opening, monthly) | >95% of category budget with work remaining | Contingency release protocol; re-tender remaining packages; T2/T3 gate review with investors |
| Maintenance cost per vehicle-hour | >$4.00 for 2 consecutive months | Volume 7 failure-data review; supplier/QC audit (Volume 8); fleet-class retirement review |
| Price test results (any §8.3 experiment) | Contribution-negative at 95% confidence | Revert within one week; elasticity belief updated in this chapter's next revision |
| FX (USD-RMB) or freight index | ±15% vs plan | Forward-order 2 quarters of spares (≈$25 K working capital); re-quote across Volume 8's second-supplier matrix |

## 10. Growth Scenarios

### 10.1 Conservative / base / ambitious — five-year view

Assumptions differ only on the demand side and phasing pace; the cost machinery (Chapter 5) and cost-flex ladder (§6.5) apply in all three. The base case **is** the canon of Chapters 4–7.

| Assumption | Conservative | Base | Ambitious |
|---|---|---|---|
| Year 1 visits | ≈31 K (−20%) | ≈39 K | ≈46 K (+18%) |
| 90-day second-visit rate | 17% | 22% | 28% |
| End-Y1 members | 220 | 344 | 470 |
| Phase 2 timing | Gated: delayed to Months 19–36, Marine-first descope | Months 13–30 | On schedule, restaurant pulled forward 3 months |
| Phase 3 | Deferred indefinitely (arena case fails hurdle) | Months 37–60 selective | Full program + franchise pilot at Month 36 |
| Blended per-cap spend trend | Flat $28 | $30 → $33 | $31 → $36 |

| Output ($K) | Y1 | Y2 | Y3 | Y4 | Y5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Conservative** — revenue | 1,020 | 1,450 | 1,950 | 2,250 | 2,500 |
| — EBITDA (margin) | −230 | 20 (1%) | 330 (17%) | 430 (19%) | 520 (21%) |
| **Base (canon)** — revenue | 1,280 | 1,905 | 2,600 | 3,030 | 3,400 |
| — EBITDA (margin) | −100 | 154 (8%) | 630 (24%) | 782 (26%) | 930 (27%) |
| **Ambitious** — revenue | 1,450 | 2,300 | 3,200 | 3,900 | 4,500 |
| — EBITDA (margin) | −40 | 320 (14%) | 870 (27%) | 1,090 (28%) | 1,280 (28%) |

Derived markers: break-even Month 22–26 / **16–19** / 12–14; Phase-1 payback beyond Year 5 / **Month ~53** / Month ~44 (ambitious cumulative EBITDA: −40+320+870 = 1,150 by end-Y3; 1,850−1,150 = 700 ÷ 1,090 × 12 ≈ 8 months into Year 4). Note the conservative case still reaches a **21% margin business worth roughly its invested capital** — the downside is mediocrity, not wipeout — while the ambitious case is deliberately *not* heroic: +18% Year-1 visits is inside Volume 2's funnel upside band, and its margins are capped at 28% (canon) rather than allowed to inflate.

### 10.2 Phase 3 optionality

Phase 3 is a menu, not a bundle: each element clears a standalone hurdle (incremental EBITDA ÷ element capex ≥ 25%) at the Month-30 review, funded from cash flow only. Planning estimates: **indoor arena** ($452 K) — removes the weather ceiling on ~30% of currently-lost days and unlocks winter leagues; projected +$260–340 K revenue at ~45% incremental margin → ROIC ≈ 26–34%, the strongest and most strategic case (it is also the MKT-07 structural fix from Volume 2's risk register). **Night-racing lighting** ($78 K) — +$60–90 K high-margin event revenue → ROIC ≈ 35–55%, cheapest yes. **Academy classrooms** ($108 K) — education line 60 → 100+ with school-day utilization of empty midweek capacity → ROIC ≈ 20–30%, borderline standalone but strategically loaded (feeds licensing and franchise training). **Corporate event centre** ($132 K) — corporate 205 → 240+ at high margin → ROIC ≈ 20–26%. Elements failing their hurdle at Month 30 are re-tested annually; the base case assumes all four proceed across Months 37–60 within the $900 K envelope.

### 10.3 Franchise upside (pointer to Volume 12)

Nothing in this volume's canon includes franchising, deliberately. Volume 12 develops the model — franchise fee, royalty on gross revenue, RC WORLD OS SaaS fee per site, and procurement margin via the Volume 8 supply chain — with its pilot gated on three Volume-10 facts being demonstrated at the flagship: sustained 24%+ EBITDA margin (Year 3), a documented operating system (Volumes 3–9 SOPs live in RC WORLD OS), and a replicable capex bill of materials (Chapter 2 of this volume, which doubles as the franchise build budget template). For scale: each franchised site paying a mid-single-digit royalty on revenues comparable to this park's Year-3 canon would contribute high-five to low-six figures of near-pure-margin annual royalty — economics equivalent to adding a division for zero capex. Treat every franchise dollar as upside to §7.5's returns, not as plan.

### 10.4 KPI dashboard definition

The park is managed on ten numbers, computed continuously by RC WORLD OS (implementation: Volume 13, Chapter 9; review cadence: weekly ops, monthly board). Definitions are fixed here so every volume and every site computes them identically.

| KPI | Definition (exact) | Y1 target | Y3 target |
|---|---|---|---|
| RevPASH (revenue per available Shift-hour) | Shift & session revenue ÷ (concurrent stations × operating hours). Y1: 786.2 K ÷ (57 × 8 × 360) = **$4.79** | ≥ $4.75 | ≥ $6.50 (74 stations post-Phase 2: 1,390 K ÷ 213,120 = $6.52) |
| Slot utilization | Blocks consumed ÷ slot capacity (§4.3). Y1: 57,720 ÷ 328,320 = **17.6%** | ≥ 17% | ≥ 24% |
| Membership count / churn | Active members at month-end / cancellations ÷ opening members | 344 / ≤3.5%/mo | ~620 avg / ≤2.5%/mo |
| 90-day second-visit rate | First-time visitors returning within 90 days (cohort-tracked) | ≥ 22% | ≥ 28% |
| Maintenance cost per vehicle-hour | Total §5.2 fleet cost ÷ telemetry-logged vehicle-hours. Y1: 66,000 ÷ 20,000 = **$3.30** | ≤ $3.50 | ≤ $3.40 |
| Fleet availability | Fleet-hours in `active` status ÷ scheduled fleet-hours (from `fleet_inventory`) | ≥ 92% | ≥ 94% |
| F&B attach | F&B revenue ÷ gate visits. Y1: 158 K ÷ 42 K = **$3.76** | ≥ $3.75 | ≥ $4.40 (restaurant) |
| Per-cap spend | (Total revenue − sponsorship − education) ÷ gate visits | ≥ $30 | ≥ $33 |
| Labor ratio | People cost ÷ revenue (§5.1) | ≤ 60% | ≤ 41% |
| NPS | Standard survey, pushed post-visit via app | ≥ 55 | ≥ 60 |

> **Investor Note.** Insist on this dashboard in the monthly pack from opening week, and on the definitions above rather than management-friendly variants. The first two KPIs (RevPASH and utilization) are the earliest honest indicators of whether the Chapter 4 engine is performing — they move weeks before revenue misses become visible — and the second-visit rate is the single best predictor of whether Year 2–3 canon is reachable, because everything in the growth model (§4.9) is frequency, not reach.

## 11. Volume summary & cross-references

This volume built RC WORLD's complete financial system and reconciled every output to the canonical headlines. **Capex:** Phase 1 builds bottom-up to $1,850 K across nine audited categories plus 10% contingency, with the striking structural fact that the entire ~150-asset fleet is only $80 K (4.3%) of it; Phase 2 ($1,150 K) and Phase 3 ($900 K) envelopes complete the ≈$3.9 M five-year program. **Funding:** the $2.6 M ask = $1,850 K capex + $750 K of working capital, operating funding, and reserve, drawn in three milestone-gated tranches ($1,200/$850/$550 K), with Phases 2–3 self-funded from cash flow plus an optional $600 K facility. **Revenue:** a bottom-up engine (39 K paid visits, 57 stations, 17.6% utilization, the canonical price card) lands Year 1 at $1,280 K monthly-reconciled, and the five-year table at $1,905 K / **$2,600 K** / $3,030 K / **$3,400 K** — agreeing independently with Volume 2's market-side estimate. **Costs and margin:** an $1,380 K Year-1 stack (60% people-weighted) grows only $590 K while revenue grows $1,320 K to Year 3, delivering EBITDA of −$100 K / $154 K / $630 K / $782 K / $930 K and the canonical **24–28% margin from Year 3**. **Cash:** the monthly model shows sustained operating break-even at **Month 16** (canonical band 16–19), a minimum cash of $476 K against a $250 K policy floor, and a closed five-year sources-and-uses at $5,596 K. **Returns:** payback **Year 4–5** (base Month ~53 on Phase 1 capital), base-case investor MOIC 1.6–2.0× / IRR 8–12.5% with conservative-case capital protection and ambitious-plus-franchise upside to ≈2.9× / ≈19%.

# RC WORLD Master Development Plan — Volume 11: Architecture & Park Design

**Volume 11 of 13** · **Revision:** 1.0 — July 2026 · **Status:** Living document — bump revision on material change

**Purpose of this volume.** This volume is the architects' and contractors' brief for the RC WORLD park: the master site plan for the canonical 4.8-hectare reference site, dimensioned zone-by-zone design concepts, building floor plans with room schedules, utilities and infrastructure concepts, and the safety, security and landscape systems that bind them together. It translates the operating doctrine of Volumes 3–7 — sight-line separation, the 15° haul-road limit, the bunkered charging doctrine, the fully netted airfield, the 20-minute Shift throughput model — into buildable geometry: areas in m², heights in mm, gradients in degrees and percent, electrical loads in kVA. It is written so that a design team can take it, a topographic survey, and the local code set, and proceed directly to schematic design. Where this volume states a dimension, every other volume must quote it; where another volume is named as source of truth (fleet counts, pond depth, cage envelope), this volume quotes *it* and says so.

**Intended readers.** The appointed architect, civil/structural engineer, MEP engineer and landscape architect; the main contractor and specialist net/pond/track subcontractors; the founder and General Manager acting as informed client; investors and lenders assessing the physical asset behind the Phase 1 capex (≈ $1.85 M, Volume 10); franchisees adapting the reference design under Volume 12; the permitting consultant preparing planning and building submissions.

**A note on codes.** RC WORLD is planned for a mid-size international city not yet fixed; this volume therefore specifies *performance and geometry*, not statutory compliance. Every item flagged **[verify locally]** — occupancy classifications, fire separations, sanitary fixture counts, accessible-parking ratios, electrical standards, structural wind/seismic loads, pond safety barriers — must be confirmed against the governing local code by the appointed design team before construction documents. Nothing in this volume overrides local law.

## 1. Design Philosophy & Site Selection

### 1.1 The park is the product: industrial-authentic, not theme-park

RC WORLD sells the fantasy of operating a working industrial complex at 1/14 scale. The architecture must therefore *be* industrial, not depict it. The design language is *industrial-authentic*: real materials doing real jobs, detailed honestly, weathering gracefully, photographing like a documentary rather than a stage set. Three consequences follow.

**First, the materials palette is the working world's palette.** Scaffold-tube guardrails, shipping containers as enclosed program, corten and galvanized steel, board-marked and power-floated concrete, timber sleepers, HDPE shade sails in plant colors (safety yellow, machine orange, gunmetal). Nothing is painted to look like something else. A container that houses the marine plant room is labeled MARINE PLANT ROOM in stenciled DIN lettering, because that is what a port operator would do — and the stencil *is* the theming.

| Element | Canonical material & finish | Where used |
|---|---|---|
| Guardrails & operator rails | 42 mm galvanized scaffold tube, key-clamp fittings, rail height 1.1 m (operator) / 1.1–1.2 m (spectator) | All zones, walkways, rostrums |
| Enclosed program (plant, stores, kiosks) | 20 ft / 40 ft high-cube shipping containers, corten patina or RAL 7016/1023 repaint, container-code graphics retained | Marine plant, parts overflow, F&B kiosk, marshal posts |
| Feature cladding & signage plates | 1.5–3 mm corten steel sheet, laser-cut lettering, unfinished | Zone gateways, wayfinding totems, hopper cladding |
| Walking surfaces | Compacted crushed stone (guest paths), power-floated concrete (buildings, pit lane), timber boardwalk (crawler zone, pond quay) | Site-wide |
| Retaining & pit edges | New/reclaimed timber sleepers 200 × 100 mm, galvanized pin fixings | Mining rim, berms, planters |
| Shade | HDPE knitted shade sails, 90%+ UV block, on 76–114 mm galvanized posts | Operator stations, rostrums, queues |
| Roofs (buildings) | Trapezoidal profile steel sheet, 6° min pitch, exposed gutters and downpipes to visible rainwater channels | The Works, entry pavilion, restaurant |

> **Field Note** — The cheapest theming decision in the whole park is *restraint*. Every fake rock, cartoon graphic or plastic-log fence added "for the kids" dilutes the premium that Volume 2's market research identified: adults pay because the place feels like a real site they are finally allowed to run. Kids do not need help pretending; adults do. Build for the adults' disbelief and the kids come free.

**Second, scale discipline.** The park operates two scales simultaneously: 1:1 for humans (rails, counters, doors) and roughly 1/14 for the machine world (dig faces, crop rows, quay bollards). The two must never blur. Human furniture is deliberately plain and industrial so the eye reads it as "backstage"; the machine world is detailed to scale-model fidelity (Volume 2, Chapter 4 sources the dressing; Volume 4 specifies the mining scenography). Rule of thumb for designers: *anything a camera at machine height can see is scenography and must be to scale; anything only a standing human sees is plant and must be honest.*

**Third, the sight-line doctrine: see everything, touch nothing live.** This is the load-bearing safety idea of the entire park, inherited from the source doctrine (customers never walk onto live tracks; Tow-Truck Retrieval Protocol instead) and it is architectural before it is procedural:

- Every operator station gives an unaided, unobstructed view of the operator's machine and its full working envelope — no station may require operating into a visual shadow (this rule fixed the mining hopper's position, Volume 4, Chapter 6).
- Every live surface (track, pit, pond, cage, field) is separated from guests by a physical edge — rail, fence, level change, water — of at least 1.1 m effective height, with kick-plates where objects could roll under. Gates into live areas are staff-controlled and interlocked with zone status in RC WORLD OS.
- Spectating is a designed product, not a leftover: terraces, mounds, the grandstand, and the elevated mining walkway (Chapter 9) are placed so that a non-paying companion always has somewhere good to stand, in shade, with the action framed for a phone camera. Volume 2's finding that "media is the marketing department" is implemented here as geometry.
- Nothing that is live is reachable, and nothing that is reachable is live. Dead vehicles are retrieved by the recovery crawlers (gameplay) or by staff; the architecture removes the temptation by making the reach physically impossible, not merely forbidden.

> **Safety Warning** — The 1.1 m rail is the *minimum effective* barrier height and assumes level standing ground on the guest side. Wherever guests stand on raised terraces, mounds or walkways, the barrier must be re-derived from the local fall/reach condition and checked against the governing building code **[verify locally]**. The sight-line doctrine never justifies lowering a barrier; if a rail blocks a child's view, the ground is raised (step, mound) — the rail is not lowered.

### 1.2 Design tenets for every consultant

1. **Throughput is geometry.** The 20-minute Shift model (canon) means every attraction is sized around simultaneous stations × turnover, not around track length or pond area for their own sake. Queue, briefing, hand-over and retrieval space is program, not circulation.
2. **Maintenance access is a first-class user.** Every zone has a staff-side service edge reachable by the utility vehicles and, for mining/marine/airfield, by a light truck. If an Artisan cannot reach a feature with a toolbag in under two minutes, redesign it.
3. **Phase lines are clean lines.** Phase 2 and 3 works (Chapter 2.4) must be buildable behind construction fencing without closing Phase 1 zones or crossing guest circulation. Utilities are stubbed to phase boundaries at Phase 1 (Chapter 12).
4. **Design for the hose and the broom.** Dust, mud and water are the park's daily weather. Falls to drainage everywhere, no un-drained low points, washdown points at every zone, surfaces that a leaf-blower and a hose can reset in 30 minutes each morning.
5. **Wind is a program input.** The airfield's orientation, the pond's sheltering berms and the shade-sail engineering all begin from the site wind rose (Section 1.4 checklist; Volume 5, Chapter 2 and Volume 6, Chapter 2 state the operating wind limits this plan must protect).

### 1.3 The canonical reference site

All dimensions in this volume are laid out on the **canonical reference site** (style-guide canon): **4.8 hectares (~12 acres)** of leased peri-urban land in a mid-size international city; **flat, with a 2–4% natural grade** falling to the southwest corner; **road frontage** on the southern boundary; **municipal three-phase power and water** at the frontage. The reference plat is taken as a rectangle **240 m (E–W) × 200 m (N–S)** = 48,000 m²; a real site of different proportion re-flows the master plan (Chapter 2) but must preserve the adjacency logic, the noise gradient, and every zone's internal dimensions.

The 2–4% grade is an asset, not a defect: it drains the site to a single southwest detention point (Chapter 11), gives the mining rim its elevation for free at the north end, and is imperceptible to guests. Sites steeper than ~5% average impose retaining costs that break the Phase 1 budget; sites dead flat impose drainage pumping. The band is deliberate.

### 1.4 Site-selection criteria checklist

The following checklist is the go/no-go filter for the reference site and for every franchise site under Volume 12. Items marked ● are hard requirements; ○ are strong preferences that trade against each other.

- [ ] ● **Area:** ≥ 4.5 ha contiguous and developable (4.8 ha reference); regular shape, no dimension < 150 m.
- [ ] ● **Grade:** average natural grade 1–5%; no more than 15% of the site steeper than 8%.
- [ ] ● **Frontage & access:** direct frontage to a public road able to take coaches and articulated delivery vehicles; sight distances at the access point adequate for a leisure use **[verify locally]**.
- [ ] ● **Power:** municipal three-phase supply at or near the frontage, upgradeable to ≥ 200 kVA demand (Chapter 12 load schedule); note the utility's connection lead time in the project program.
- [ ] ● **Water & sewer:** municipal potable water at frontage; sewer connection or approved on-site treatment feasible **[verify locally]**.
- [ ] ● **Planning/zoning:** leisure/recreation use permitted or realistically permittable; no residential facade within 100 m of the northern (operational) half of the plan, or acoustic report demonstrates compliance **[verify locally]**.
- [ ] ● **Flood:** outside the locally defined high-risk flood zone; if in a moderate zone, finished floor levels and the detention strategy (Chapter 11) resolve it **[verify locally]**.
- [ ] ● **Tenure:** lease ≥ 10 years with renewal option, or purchase; landlord consent for the netted airfield's 16–17 m poles obtained in principle before signing.
- [ ] ○ **Catchment:** ≥ 500,000 population within 45 minutes' drive (Volume 2, Chapter 7 demand model).
- [ ] ○ **Wind:** 12-month wind rose available or commissioned; prevailing direction steady enough to orient the airfield within ±20° (Volume 5 canon); mean speeds compatible with marine operating windows (Volume 6).
- [ ] ○ **Soil:** free-draining granular soils preferred (tracks, pond excavation, pole foundations); a Phase 0 geotechnical investigation with ≥ 6 trial pits and 2 boreholes at the airfield and arena positions is a pre-contract requirement.
- [ ] ○ **Aviation constraints:** site outside airport obstacle-limitation surfaces and any UAS restriction zone that would prohibit even netted model flight; confirm the 17 m poles trigger no aviation-obstacle process **[verify locally]**.
- [ ] ○ **Neighbours:** no dust-sensitive or noise-sensitive neighbour (hospital, kennel, precision industry) sharing the northern boundary.
- [ ] ○ **Visibility:** frontage visible to passing traffic (the netted cage and corten gateway are the billboard).
- [ ] ○ **Transit & coach:** public transport stop within 500 m; school-coach approach without reversing.

> **Investor Note** — Volume 2 identified land as a structural barrier to entry: 4–5 contiguous peri-urban hectares with utilities are scarce exactly where demand is strongest. The checklist above is deliberately strict; a site that fails two ● items is a walk-away regardless of price, because every failure lands in Phase 1 capex or in the operating calendar (wind, flood) forever.

## 2. Master Site Plan

### 2.1 Allocation: 48,000 m² fully accounted

The master plan allocates every square meter of the 4.8 ha reference site. Areas are *precinct* areas — the zone plus its own internal service edge and immediate spectator edge; park-wide guest circulation and landscape are carried as their own lines. Guest circulation is **13% of the developed area**, inside the 12–15% band that keeps peak-day flows one-way capable (Chapter 9).

Two ratios matter for review discipline. **Attraction : support** — precincts 3–9 and 12–13 (the paid experiences) total 18,950 m², 39.5% of site; if value-engineering ever pushes this below ~35% the park has become a car park with hobbies attached. **Hard : soft** — sealed and roofed surfaces total ≈ 31% of site at Phase 3 build-out, which the stormwater strategy (Chapter 11) is sized for; any increase re-opens the detention calculation.

### 2.2 Adjacency logic

The plan is an argument, and each adjacency is a clause of it:

- **Mining borders The Works** (precincts 7 and 9 share an edge) because the Construction Division has the park's heaviest assets, the highest per-Shift maintenance event rate (Volume 4), and the only bulk-material logistics: aggregate top-ups, hopper maintenance and the nightly face re-cut all run from The Works' yard through a single staff gate. The mining hopper sits at the zone's east end (fixed in Volume 4 by the sight-line rule) — which is exactly the Works-facing end, so the conveyor and weighbridge electronics are a 20 m walk from the electronics bench.
- **The Works sits on the eastern service spine**, front door facing the guest path (the viewing window, Chapter 6, makes Artisan work a spectacle), back door facing the service road, so parts deliveries and fleet movements never cross a guest route.
- **The Airfield is peripheral and downwind: the northeast corner.** Three independent reasons converge. (1) *Risk geometry* — although the cage makes flyaway physically contained (Volume 5), defense in depth wants maximum distance between flight operations and both the entry crowds and the public road. (2) *Noise* — EDF and prop noise is the park's loudest continuous source; with the prevailing southwesterly of the reference wind rose, the northeast corner exports noise away from the entry, the restaurant and the frontage neighbours. (3) *Structure* — the 16–17 m poles (Volume 5 canon) want the longest possible setback from the boundary the planning authority cares about, which is the road frontage. The cage's long axis runs E–W, within the ±20° of prevailing wind that Volume 5 requires.
- **Marine and Agriculture are the calm band**, west-center, adjacent to each other: the two quietest, most family-skewed zones share the gentlest part of the noise gradient, the events lawn, and the afternoon shade of the western berm. The pond sits in the wind shadow engineered by that berm (Volume 6 makes wind shelter a revenue item).
- **Track A fronts the social heart.** The asphalt track is the park's most legible spectacle, so it sits center-east where the pit lane, grandstand and (Phase 2) restaurant terrace all overlook it. The drag straight aligns with the grandstand's axis.
- **Track B and Track C occupy the northwest**, between Agriculture and Mining: dirt with dirt. Their dust sources sit downwind of the guest core on the prevailing wind and their service needs share the northern staff route.
- **Entry, parking and the Phase 3 arena hold the south frontage.** Everything a visitor does before paying — parking, drop-off, ticketing — stays south of the guest gateway; the arena (Phase 3) also fronts south so corporate-event traffic never enters the park proper.

### 2.3 The noise gradient

Sound is planned as a south-to-north crescendo. At the frontage: car doors and café murmur. Through the gateway: PA at conversation level, the pond's calm. Mid-park: Track A tire noise and commentary. North band: mining buzzers, Track B's jumps, the airfield's motors — all held against the northern landscape berm (Chapter 11), which is both acoustic screen and viewing mound. Design targets, to be confirmed by the acoustic consultant against local limits **[verify locally]**: ≤ 55 dB(A) LAeq at the southern boundary, ≤ 50 dB(A) at any residential facade. The gradient also works commercially: the entry experience stays unhurried (retail dwell), and anticipation builds as guests walk north into the machine noise.

### 2.4 Phased build overlay

| Phase | Occupies | Construction access | Guest impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Phase 1 (Months 0–12)** | Precincts 1–11: entry + parking core (88 car bays), Tracks A/B/C, pit lane + charging, Mining, Agriculture, The Works, Phase 1 circulation and berms. Utilities trunk routes laid full-length with stubs at Phase 2/3 boundaries. | Full site is a construction site | — |
| **Phase 2 (Months 13–30)** | Precincts 12–16: airfield cage, marine basins, restaurant, grandstand + events lawn, parking extension (+44 bays). | NE and W-center parcels, fenced; heavy deliveries (poles, liner, precast) via the eastern service road out of guest hours | Zero closure of Phase 1 zones; crane lifts for airfield poles scheduled on closed days |
| **Phase 3 (Months 31–60)** | Precincts 17–18: indoor arena + academy + corporate centre (SE), night-racing lighting retrofit on Tracks A/B, franchise-pilot support space. | SE parcel direct from frontage — never enters the park | Lighting works at night behind track closures |

The phase lines were drawn so that each later phase is a *parcel*, not a scatter: one construction fence, one gate, one insurance boundary. Phase 1 tenders should price the Phase 2 duct and drainage stubs as provisional sums — they cost hundreds now and tens of thousands if retro-trenched through a live park.

**Tender packaging.** Phase 1 splits naturally into six packages, and splitting them is a cost decision, not just a program one — three of the six are specialist trades a general contractor would only mark up:

| Package | Scope | Procurement route |
|---|---|---|
| P1-A Civils & earthworks | Bulk cut/fill, berms, pit excavation, roads, drainage, ducts, bases | Main contractor |
| P1-B Buildings | The Works, entry pavilion, pit building shell | Main contractor (same tender as P1-A) |
| P1-C Track surfaces | Track A asphalt/concrete + kerbs; Track B clay-gravel system | Specialist paving sub, direct — surface tolerance is the product |
| P1-D Zone fit-out & scenography | Sleeper works, hopper, barn/silo, dressing packages (Volume 2 supplier channel), rails, sails | Direct trades + Volume 8 procurement |
| P1-E MEP & data | Boards, sub-boards, bunker electrical, Wi-Fi/CCTV/PA, comms room | MEP contractor, designed by the MEP engineer |
| P1-F Loose & operational | Rostrum systems, barriers, signage, furniture | Direct purchase, Artisan-installed where possible |

Phase 2 adds two more specialist directs: the **net system** (design-build by a netting engineer against Volume 5's performance spec — never let a general contractor "equal-or-approve" a life-safety net) and the **pond liner** (installed by the membrane manufacturer's approved crew, with the warranty tied to their installation). The client-side rule across all packages: any substitution touching a hold-point dimension (handover checklist) routes through the founder and this volume's change register, not through site instructions.

## 3. Zone Design — Motorsport

The Speed & Off-Road Hub is three engineered surfaces plus the shared driver infrastructure. Volume 3 owns everything about the cars and the racing program; this chapter owns everything you can pour, compact, bolt or plant. Where Volume 3 stated interface requirements (its Sections 9.6, 10.4, 11.4, 13.2), they are restated here as built geometry.

### 3.1 Track A — asphalt/drift circuit

**Layout geometry.** Track A is a closed circuit of **~180 m racing line** within a 60 × 45 m precinct pad, designed bidirectional (Volume 3 canon: league nights may invert direction, so barrier profiles, kerb ramps and rostrum sight lines are symmetrical about the racing line). The canonical layout:

| Parameter | Specification |
|---|---|
| Racing line length | 180 m (–0/+10 m as built; report as-built to Volume 3 for lap-parity math) |
| Lane width | **3.5 m minimum, 4.5 m** on the main straight and outside of Turn 1 (widest where speeds are highest and passing is intended) |
| Main straight | **58 m** between corner tangent points — satisfies the ≥ 55 m drag requirement: 40.2 m strip + ≥ 15 m braking run-off (Volume 3 canon) |
| Corner set | 8 corners: T1 R=6.0 m 90°; T2–T3 chicane R=3.0 m; T4 hairpin R=2.5 m (minimum radius on circuit); T5 R=8.0 m sweeper 120°; T6 R=4.0 m; T7–T8 esses R=3.5 m onto the straight |
| Minimum corner radius | 2.5 m (hairpin) — below 2.0 m, 1/10 touring cars scrub instead of steer |
| Crossfall | 1.5–2.0% uniform to the outside edge (drainage; imperceptible to handling at this scale) |
| Drift annex | 15 × 12 m polished pad joined at T5, own entry gate, sharing the T5 sweep as a linked layout (Volume 3, Section 9.6) |

**Surface build-up (section, top down):** 25–30 mm fine-graded asphalt wearing course (6 mm nominal aggregate, machine-laid — hand-laid asphalt leaves grip inconsistencies the parity program will find) *or* 120 mm power-floated concrete slab with a light mechanical polish on the drift annex; 150 mm compacted crushed-stone base (CBR ≥ 30); compacted subgrade; geotextile separator on soft spots. Joints in the concrete option are sawn, not tooled, and sealed flush — a 3 mm lip is a launch ramp at 1/10 scale. Surface tolerance: 3 mm under a 3 m straightedge anywhere on the racing line.

**Kerbs.** Corner apexes and exit edges carry **scale FIA-profile kerbs**: precast concrete or machined HDPE strips 300 mm wide, rising 15 mm at 1:10 chamfer, painted red/white in 250 mm alternations. Kerbs are glued and pinned, not just bedded — a loose kerb is a projectile. The kerb face never exceeds 15 mm: at 60 km/h a 1/10 car treats 15 mm as a rumble, 25 mm as a wall.

**Run-off and barriers, in order of energy absorbed:** (1) painted run-off apron 0.5–1.0 m wide in the same surface, (2) a 0.3 m crushed-rubber-granule strip at high-energy corners (T1, T4, end of straight), then (3) the **barrier system**: 200 mm diameter foam pool-noodle-over-rope barrier on 12 mm polypropylene rope threaded through galvanized eye stakes at 1.0 m centers — the industry-standard RC track barrier, cheap, continuous, and energy-absorbing with no hard edges. Behind it, at the spectator edge only, a rigid 1.1 m scaffold-tube rail with 150 mm timber kick-plate. The two-stage system means a 60 km/h drag car meets foam first, steel never. Marshal access gaps every 15 m, offset so no straight-line path from track to public exists.

**Embedded services (cast in at construction, per Volume 3):** MYLAPS RC4 timing-loop conduit (25 mm) across start/finish plus a spare loop conduit mid-straight for the drag trap; 50 mm power/data conduit ring for trackside cameras and (Phase 3) floodlighting; drainage channel at the low edge discharging to the swale network (Chapter 11).

**Construction sequence and QA hold points.** Track A is the one surface in the park where the contractor's habits from full-scale roadwork actively mislead: tolerances that pass on a highway fail here. Sequence: (1) subgrade proof-roll, witnessed; (2) base course laid and compacted to ≥ 98% modified Proctor, surveyed on a 5 m grid, ±10 mm; (3) timing and lighting conduits set and *sleeved through, not under*, the base; (4) wearing course machine-laid in maximum two passes with a hot longitudinal joint on the racing line's least-loaded axis — never mid-corner; (5) 72-hour cure/traffic hold; (6) acceptance survey: **3 mm under a 3 m straightedge anywhere on the racing line, no ponding after a hose test, joint lips ≤ 1 mm**. A failed panel is cut back to the nearest joint and re-laid — surface patching is prohibited on the racing line because the parity program (Volume 3, lap times within 2–3%) will detect a grip patch faster than any straightedge. The drift annex's mechanical polish is a separate visit after cure, with a skid-value target set jointly with the Motorsport Lead from test-car sessions: polish is sneaking up on a number, not executing a spec.

### 3.2 Track B — dirt rally circuit

**Layout geometry.** ~**160 m racing line** in a 55 × 42 m precinct, packed-dirt surface, 4.0 m nominal width (4.5 m on the jump straight), designed unidirectional (jumps have a direction; inverting Track B is forbidden — the landing ramps only work one way).

**Surface engineering.** 100 mm of screened clay-bound gravel ("road base with fines", 10–15% clay fraction) laid over 100 mm compacted crushed stone, watered and rolled to a hard, slightly plastic running crust. The clay fraction is the maintenance variable: too little and the surface ravels to marbles, too much and rain closes the track. The track crew's daily water-and-roll reset (Volume 3, Section 10.4 moisture doctrine: "dark but not shiny") is enabled by a dedicated hose ring with take-offs every 20 m and a walk-behind roller garaged at the zone.

**Jump profiles and the safe-landing ratio.** All jumps are **tabletops** (never doubles — a cased double destroys rental fleet at industrial rates; a cased tabletop is just a flat landing) built to Volume 3's canon of **≤ 0.5 m height, landing-matched**:

| Element | Dimension | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Take-off ramp | Rise 0.5 m over 1.5 m run (18°) with the last 300 mm relaxed to 12° | The relaxed lip stops rental buggies from over-rotating; a sharp lip is a backflip machine |
| Table (deck) | 2.5 m level | Cars landing short land flat |
| Landing ramp | Fall 0.5 m over **2.5 m** run (11°) | **Landing length ≥ 5 × jump height** — the safe-landing ratio this volume fixes. At the 50 km/h rental cap, flight is 3–5 m; an 11° landing matches the descent angle so suspension absorbs mm, not the chassis |
| Transition radii | ≥ 1.0 m at ramp toe and crest | No kinks: a kink is a load spike |
| Construction | Compacted fill core faced with 75 mm clay-gravel wearing layer over geogrid; timber-sleeper edge boards flush with surface | Jumps that shrink under traffic become doubles by erosion — the geogrid and edge boards hold profile |

Two tabletops sit on the jump straight, one single "kicker" tabletop at 0.3 m height on the back section. A whoops section (five rollers, 150 mm high at 1.2 m pitch) provides the technical suspension test without airtime.

**Berm construction.** Bermed corners are the dirt track's kerbs: compacted fill banks on the outside of corners T2, T5 and T7, **inner radius per corner (2.5–5 m), bank face rising to 400 mm at 30–35°**, faced with the same clay-gravel wearing course over a geogrid-wrapped core, sleeper-edged at the back. Berms are cut with a 100 mm flat shelf at the top so an overshooting car parks rather than launches. Rebuild profile is checked monthly against painted depth gauges set in the berm core.

**Drainage.** Dirt tracks die by water. The whole precinct is crowned at 2% to perimeter french drains (100 mm perforated pipe in 300 × 300 mm gravel trench, geotextile-wrapped) discharging to the northern swale; jump and berm cores are free-draining fill so they don't slump; and the marshal posts stand on 100 mm raised concrete pads (Volume 3 requires them splash-safe). After the design storm the track must be rollable within 2 hours — that criterion, not a pipe size, is the spec the civil engineer must meet **[verify locally]** for local rainfall intensity.

### 3.3 Track C — crawler park

Track C serves the 16-crawler fleet (Volume 4 program ownership) on a **40 × 30 m (1,200 m²)** terrain garden: the park's slowest zone and its highest dwell-per-square-meter. Design speed is walking pace; danger is near zero; the design problem is *interest density* and operator sight lines.

**Layout.** A figure-eight trail network (~90 m of marked lines, 600 mm lane width) through a landscape of feature stations, with operators following their crawlers along a raised timber boardwalk spine (1.2 m wide, 300 mm above grade, 1.1 m rail on the terrain side) — the one zone where guests move *with* their machines. Boardwalk and trail never cross at grade; the trail passes under boardwalk bridges.

**Feature catalogue** (each feature is numbered, difficulty-rated 1–5 in RC WORLD OS, and buildable/replaceable as a unit):

| # | Feature | Dimensions | Difficulty | Construction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Boulder garden | 8 × 4 m field, stones 100–400 mm | 2–4 | Sorted natural stone, largest pieces pinned with dowel and epoxy |
| C2 | Rock steps ascent | 6 steps, 120–180 mm rise each, total climb 0.9 m | 3 | Flat-faced stone bedded in dry-pack mortar |
| C3 | Timber bridge pair | Spans 1.8 m and 2.4 m, deck 350 mm wide, no rails (fall 300 mm to sand) | 2/4 | 100 × 50 mm treated timber, wire-brushed for grip |
| C4 | Log crossing | Half-round logs 150–250 mm dia., 3 m run | 4 | Fixed with hidden pins; replace when polished smooth |
| C5 | Water hazard — ford | 1.2 m wide crossing, **max depth 80 mm** | 3 | Lined concrete dish, textured invert |
| C6 | Water hazard — pool skirt | 2 × 3 m pool, trail on submerged shelf, **max depth 120 mm** at trail, 200 mm at center (no trail line through center) | 4 | EPDM-lined, pump-recirculated from the crawler zone sump |
| C7 | Scree slope | 4 m at 25°, loose 10 mm gravel over fixed base | 5 | Contained by sleeper edge; gravel topped up weekly |
| C8 | Teeter bridge | 2.0 m pivoting plank, 400 mm max tip | 5 | Steel pivot, rubber stops; the signature photo feature |
| C9 | Sand wash | 6 × 2 m fine-sand basin | 2 | The beginners' loop centerpiece |
| C10 | Tunnel & culvert | 600 mm dia. half-pipe, 2 m long | 1 | Concrete pipe section; kids' favourite, keep sight line through it |

**Water-hazard depth limits are a fleet-protection spec, not a safety-of-life spec** (no water on Track C exceeds 200 mm): the rental crawler electronics (Volume 4 upfit: conformal-coated Nodes, splash-resistant ESCs) tolerate 80–120 mm fording indefinitely but not submersion, so **no trail line may exceed 120 mm water depth** and the 200 mm pool center is off-line by geometry. Both water features drain to the sump nightly in frost season **[verify locally]** for the climate's freeze regime.

### 3.4 Driver rostrums

Each track has a **driver rostrum**: an elevated stand giving drivers the commanding view that separates racing from guessing.

| Parameter | Track A | Track B | Track C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Capacity | 10 drivers (Volume 3 canon) | 8 drivers | boardwalk-integrated (no fixed rostrum) |
| Deck height | 1.2 m above track datum | 1.5 m (jumps need more angle) | 0.3 m boardwalk |
| Deck size | 12.0 × 2.4 m | 9.6 × 2.4 m | — |
| Position | Outside the main straight, mid-length, set back 2.0 m from the barrier | Outside the jump straight | — |
| Structure | Galvanized scaffold system or steel sub-frame, timber deck, 1.1 m front rail with padded transmitter ledge (300 mm wide, 15° tilt), rear rail and single 1.2 m-wide stair + accessible ramp 1:12 | same | — |
| Shade | Full-cover HDPE sail, 90% block | same | sail clusters over feature stations |

Driver positions are marked at **1.2 m centers** — elbow room for transmitter steering wheels. Rostrum sight-line check (mandatory at design review): from a 10th-percentile adult eye height at every marked position, the entire racing line is visible, including the far side of every berm and the landing of every jump. On Track A, bidirectional running means the check is done both ways.

### 3.5 Racing pit lane (trackside)

The racing pit lane serves Tracks A and B jointly, located between them at the rostrum end (the customer-facing pit *theatre* and charging station are Chapter 7; this is the working lane where Artisans stage, swap and re-issue fleet).

```
        TRACK A main straight ────────────────────────────────▶
   ═════ barrier ═══════╦═ pit entry (gate, interlocked) ═╦════
    ┌──────────────────┐║  PIT LANE  3.0 m one-way ▶      ║
    │  ROSTRUM A       │║ ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ ║
    │  10 positions    │║ │ B1 │ B2 │ B3 │ B4 │ B5 │ B6 │ ║
    │  12.0 × 2.4 m    │║ └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘ ║
    └──────────────────┘║   bays 2.0 × 1.2 m, bench-backed ║
   ══════════════════════╩══ staff spine to charging stn ══╩══
```

| Element | Dimension | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Pit lane | 3.0 m wide, one-way, power-floated concrete | Wide enough for a staff trolley + kneeling Artisan |
| Pit bays | 6 bays, **2.0 m wide × 1.2 m deep** each | One car + one Artisan + parts caddy; bay number painted, task lighting over each |
| Bench | Continuous 600 mm-deep bench at 900 mm height along the back of bays | ESD mat at bays 1–2 (electronics triage) |
| Power | Double GPO + USB-C at every bay on a dedicated 20 A circuit | No charging in the pit lane — packs move to the charging station (Ch. 7); doctrine, not convenience |
| Access | Interlocked gates to each track; roller door to the staff spine | Gate state visible in RC WORLD OS zone dashboard |

> **Trade Hack** — Cast a 100 mm-high, 300 mm-wide concrete plinth along the pit-bay front edge and set the bay floor mats on it. Cars roll in at bench-adjacent height, Artisans stop stooping, and dropped M3 screws land on mat, not gravel. Cost at pour time: nearly nothing. Retrofit cost: a weekend and an angle grinder.

## 4. Zone Design — Construction & Agriculture

Volume 4 is the operating specification for both zones and has already fixed their internal geometry; this chapter restates that geometry as construction information, adds the civil/structural detail Volume 4 delegated here, and dimensions the guest edge. Where numbers below repeat Volume 4, Volume 4 governs.

### 4.1 Mining Zone — civil design

**Envelope (Volume 4 canon):** 60 × 40 m (2,400 m²), long axis E–W, operator rim on the north edge, service spine on the south, hopper at the east end, premium pad NE. The natural grade falls SW, exploited for drainage.

**Pit cross-section.** The pit is a two-bench excavation cut below a raised operator terrace:

```
   N (guest side)                                                      S (service side)
   spectator     OPERATOR RIM                                          service
   terrace       +600 datum                                            spine ±0
  ────────┐    ┌───────────┐ rail 1.1–1.2 m
   +600   │    │ ▣ station │◁ shade sail 4×4 m
  ════════╪════╡           │
          │    └─────┬─────┘ sleeper facing, 600 mm exposed
          │          │  DIG FACE (30–40°, re-cut nightly)
          │          ▽ ─────────┐ UPPER BENCH  −300
          │                     └──────┐ bench h = 300 mm, sleeper-edged
          │                            │ LOWER PIT FLOOR  −600
          │     haul road 450 mm wide  └────────────────────────┬──────────
          │     ══ ramp 14° (canon max 15°) up to hopper apron +400 ══▷ ■ HOPPER
  ────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────
   Levels in mm relative to pit-floor datum (−600 = pit floor; rim +600; apron +400)
```

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Bench heights | Two benches: upper at −300 mm, pit floor at −600 mm; **bench step 300 mm**, sleeper-edged (200 × 100 mm sleepers, pinned) so faces re-cut nightly against a fixed line |
| Dig faces | 6 faces (DF1–DF6), 3 m wide, cut at 30–40°, one per operator pair of stations (Volume 4, Chapter 6) |
| Haul roads | 450 mm running width single-lane, 700 mm at passing bays; wearing course 20 mm compacted crusher fines over the base aggregate; **max grade 14° built (15° absolute canon limit)** on the main and return ramps — the main ramp rises −600 → +400 mm over 4.0 m of run (Volume 4) |
| Retaining edges | All level changes ≥ 300 mm on the guest side retained with timber sleeper walls, galvanized pins at 600 mm centers into compacted base; walls > 600 mm exposed get a second pinned course and a drainage gravel backfill strip |
| Rim terrace | 4 m deep compacted-gravel terrace at +600 mm, sleeper-faced; loads: crowd 5 kPa design **[verify locally]** |
| Pit floor drainage | Falls 1% to a SW sump with a lidded silt trap and a manual pump-out point; the pit is the site's lowest scenographic point but never its drainage low point |

**Hopper structure.** The central processing hopper (Volume 4, Section 6.5 owns its mechanics: 600 × 600 mm grizzly, surge bin, 2.5 m conveyor, stockpile discharge at +1.4 m) needs from this volume: a **2.5 × 2.0 m reinforced concrete plinth** at apron level (+400 mm), cast-in M12 holding-down bolts for the steel support frame, a corten cladding skin (the hopper is the zone's visual landmark and must read as plant, not as a prop), a lockable ground-level electrics cabinet (IP65) fed from the zone sub-board, and maintenance clearance of 800 mm on three sides inside the service fence.

**Operator rail stations — ergonomics.** Twelve stations at **4.0 m pitch** (Volume 4 canon) along the rim:

| Ergonomic parameter | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Rail height | **1.1 m** (1.1–1.2 m band per Volume 4) | Forearm rest for adults; chest rail for children |
| Child step | Fold-down 250 mm step, full station width | Brings a 6-year-old's eye line over the rail; folds to clear crowds |
| Transmitter shelf | 300 mm deep at 950 mm height, tilted 15°, drained slot at rear | Rests the transmitter without masking sticks; sheds rain |
| Station width | 1.5 m marked zone within the 4.0 m pitch | One operator + one leaning parent |
| Viewing angle to assigned face | 15–25° downward (Volume 4) | Deep enough to see into truck beds; shallow enough to read machine attitude at 20 m |
| Shade | 4 × 4 m HDPE sail per station pair, posts 3.2 m | LCD readability + summer dwell |
| Station furniture | Number placard, assigned-face placard, QR to live telemetry card | Volume 4, Section 6.6 |

**Material containment and recirculation.** The zone's aggregates (≈ 55 m³ initial fill: sand, pea gravel, crushed stone — Volume 4) are a closed inventory. Containment is architectural: a continuous **150 mm-high concrete edge kerb around the entire pit perimeter** at the base of all sleeper walls (material cannot migrate out at floor level), the service-spine gate has a 100 mm bump sill, and the hopper stockpile sits on a concrete saucer that the wheel loader reclaims from (Volume 4's closed material cycle). A washdown apron (2 × 3 m, falls to the silt trap) at the service gate keeps aggregate out of the park's drains — the silt trap, not the swale, is where mining fines are allowed to stop.

### 4.2 Agriculture Zone — civil design

**Envelope (Volume 4 canon):** 50 × 30 m (1,500 m²), the grid of **eight field cells at 9.0 × 5.5 m** separated by **600 mm compacted tractor lanes**, barn/silo complex on the east edge, irrigation trenches as working scenery.

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Field cells | 8 cells, 9.0 × 5.5 m each (396 m² fields total); cells F1–F4 loose tillable media 150 mm deep over a compacted base with drainage falls; F5–F6 permanent row-crop cells (row spacing 250 mm, Volume 4 materials spec); F7–F8 rotating event cells |
| Cell edging | 150 × 50 mm timber edge boards flush with lane level — a tractor must be able to cross into a field anywhere along the edge, so no upstand |
| Tractor lanes | 600 mm wide, compacted crusher fines at lane level; lane grid drains at 1% to the western swale; passing squares 1.2 × 1.2 m at grid intersections |
| Irrigation trenches | 200 mm wide × 100 mm deep lined channels along cell heads; wet by recirculating pump on show days, dry-scenic otherwise; never open water > 100 mm deep |
| Operator edge | South edge, 8 stations at 4.0 m pitch, same rail/shelf/shade ergonomics as mining (§4.1) — one detail differs: rail height 1.1 m but no child step fold-down; instead a continuous 200 mm raised timber curb-step (agriculture skews youngest, the step is always needed) |
| Barn/silo complex | Volume 4 canon: 2.4 × 1.8 m scale barn with drive-through weighbridge bay + silo tower. This volume adds: concrete plinth 3.0 × 2.4 m, barn structure in timber at scale detail (a Volume 2 diorama-supplier package), silo in rolled steel 600 mm dia. × 2.0 m, both anchored for wind **[verify locally]**, weighbridge electronics conduit back to the zone sub-board |
| Perimeter | 1.1 m post-and-rail (timber, agricultural character) with kick-plate on the guest sides; staff gate to the northern service route |

> **Field Note** — Resist the urge to "improve" the 600 mm lanes to something wider during setting-out. The lanes are gameplay: Volume 4 fixed between-row and lane clearances at ~1.4 tractor widths, and threading them clean is the zone's core skill. A contractor's generous extra 100 mm per lane quietly deletes the skill curve. The lane width is a hold-point dimension on the setting-out survey.

### 4.3 Shared service infrastructure

Both zones hang off the northern/eastern staff route: a 2.5 m-wide compacted service road linking The Works' yard, the mining service spine, the agriculture staff gate and Track B's maintenance corner. Along it: aggregate top-up bunkers (3 × 2 m sleeper bins for sand/pea/crushed — mining's replenishment stock), the walk-behind roller and hand-tool garage (20 ft container), and hose points at 40 m spacing off the irrigation main (Chapter 12). The route is fenced from guests full-length (1.5 m mesh) and gated at both ends; it doubles as the emergency vehicle route to the park's northern half (Chapter 10).
