## 5. Zone Design — Aviation & Marine

Both divisions are Phase 2 builds on parcels reserved, graded and utility-stubbed in Phase 1 (Chapter 2.4). Volume 5 owns the aviation program and the containment-engineering rationale; Volume 6 owns the marine program and the water-quality doctrine. This chapter carries the construction geometry.

### 5.1 Airfield envelope and siting

The canonical enclosure (Volume 5, Section 2.1 — the numbers every volume quotes): **flight cage 60 × 40 m footprint, 15 m clear flight ceiling, ≈ 36,000 m³ enclosed volume**, long axis aligned within ±20° of the prevailing wind, sited in the northeast quadrant per the adjacency logic of Chapter 2.2. The aviation *precinct* (allocation table line 12) is 3,400 m²: the 2,400 m² cage plus the southern spectator promenade (60 × 6 m), the pilot-access vestibule aprons, the pole maintenance strip (2 m clear around the full perimeter — scissor-lift access to every pole, non-negotiable), and the flight-line container store.

**Siting inputs the architect must fix before Phase 2 documents:** the 12-month wind rose (commissioned at Phase 1 if not already available — Volume 5 requires it and this volume's site checklist demands it), a geotechnical confirmation at each pole position, and the aviation-obstacle check for 17 m structures **[verify locally]**.

### 5.2 Net engineering

Volume 5, Section 2.2 fixes the netting specification (knotted UHMWPE #18-class or equivalent nylon, **45–48 mm mesh** walls and roof, ≥ 1.8 kN per-mesh break strength, black, UV-stabilized; 25 mm secondary skirt net at the spectator panel; ground edge sealed to < 50 mm gap). This volume adds the structure that carries it:

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Poles | Tapered galvanized steel, **16–17 m** above ground, at **10–12 m centres** (18–20 poles — Volume 5 canon); base plate on reinforced concrete pad foundations, typically ~1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 m in granular soils — final sizing by the structural engineer from site wind data and soil report **[verify locally]** |
| Roof structure | Tensioned catenary cable grid, 8–10 mm galvanized or Dyneema-core, ≤ 12 m spacing, crowned +1 m at centre (Volume 5) for sag control and rain shedding; roof net in laced panels ≈ 12 × 12 m (Volume 5 Trade Hack — panel replacement, not sheet replacement) |
| Tension system | Each perimeter cable terminated with a galvanized turnbuckle (M16 class) and a marked witness gauge; walls laced to border ropes (≥ 10 mm braided) top and bottom; **design pretension set by the net engineer so that no net face can deflect onto a flight path under working wind** — deflection check at 5 m buffer line |
| Ground seal | Bottom border rope buried 150 mm or threaded through ballast pipe full perimeter; gaps > 50 mm are a defect (Volume 5: a quad that fits under the net is not contained) |
| Access | Two personnel vestibules ≥ 2 × 2 m (double-door net airlocks) and one 3 m double-gated vehicle gate (Volume 5); vestibule doors interlocked — both never open together during flight status |
| Inspection regime | Structural: annual pole/cable/termination inspection by the engineer; nets: Volume 5's repair standard (hand-lace ≤ 3 mesh squares; panel-replace beyond) |

> **Safety Warning** — The cage is a life-safety structure with a 15–25 year design life and it fails in storms, not in operation. The structural engineer's wind analysis must model the net **iced and fouled** (leaves, snow band per climate) as a load case, and the operations manual must include a drop-or-derig wind threshold for named storms **[verify locally]** for the local wind code. A net specified only for sunny-day containment is under-specified by roughly a factor of three.

### 5.3 Runway, helipads and flight-line

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Runway | **30 × 4 m** (canon), machine-floated concrete 120 mm on 150 mm base, or fine asphalt equivalent; centreline and threshold markings in traffic paint; crossfall 1.5% to the north edge drain; surface tolerance 3 mm / 3 m |
| Overruns | 5 m mown-turf at each threshold (Volume 5 — also the EDF belly-landing strip); turf on 100 mm rootzone over free-draining base |
| Apron | 12 × 8 m concrete pad at the runway's south-east, linking the vehicle gate, the pilot boxes and the helipad edge |
| Helipads | **Two, 1.2 × 1.2 m at 0.8 m height** (Volume 5 canon), steel frame, anti-slip deck, on the apron's east edge |
| Pilot boxes | Four, in line along the runway's south side, 3 m back from pavement (Volume 5); 2.0 × 1.5 m each, 1.1 m rail, transmitter shelf per §4.1 ergonomics; the cage wall's **2 m overhead net apron** projects over the boxes so no aircraft can descend on a pilot |
| FPV race volume | Sector B per Volume 5: eastern ≈ 30 × 15 m, curtain-netted to 8 m on messenger cables, repositionable |
| Flight-line store | 20 ft container inside the cage at the vehicle gate: aircraft racking, field-repair bench, no battery charging (all charging in the bunker or the marine/aviation charging annex per doctrine) |

### 5.4 Marine basins

Volume 6 fixes the waterspace: **main basin ~40 × 25 m (1,000 m² water), 600 mm perimeter shelf grading to 800 mm central channel, ≈ 630–650 m³**; within it the **harbour basin (Zone H) 14 × 25 m** boomed off from the open-water/fast-electric area; plus the separate **8 × 6 m submarine basin at 800 mm (≈ 38 m³)**. In this volume's terms these are the **pond pair**: the *harbour pond* (Zone H, dead-slow scale operations, quay-walled) and the *speed pond* (the remaining 26 × 25 m open-water area, fast-electric and sail) sharing one liner and one plant system, with the clear-water submarine basin as an annex. **Maximum depth 800 mm everywhere, forever** — Volume 6 states it as a safety specification and this volume repeats it as a hold-point on the excavation drawings.

**Section through the main basin (E–W at the harbour):**

  ═════╪══╡ timber-faced ╞═══ waterline ═════════════┆════╪═════════════
       │  │ concrete, D- │  −600 shelf (2 m wide)    ┆    │
       │  │ fender at WL │ ─────┐                    ┆    │

A 20 ft high-cube container adjacent to the marina building, on a 100 mm bunded slab:

### 6.2 The charging bunker

The bunker implements the canonical battery doctrine (bunkered charging; 3:1 battery:vehicle ratio ⇒ ~450 packs cycling in Phase 1; LiPo window 3.4–4.2 V/cell) as architecture:

| Parameter | Specification |
|---|---|
| Construction | **Fully filled cinderblock (CMU) walls, 190 mm**, to the underside of a reinforced-concrete lid slab; internal 30 m² (6.0 × 5.0 m); no combustible linings; concrete floor with 50 mm containment sill at the door |
| Blast/fire venting | **Deliberate weak panel venting upward and outward to the yard**: two 600 × 600 mm blow-out panels high in the yard-side wall, lightweight sacrificial construction, discharging to a fenced 3 m exclusion strip — never toward an occupied room or guest area |
| Door | Single **fire-rated door (90-minute class, FD90) with self-closer**, opening outward to the corridor; signage per fire code **[verify locally]** |
| Charging plant | Industrial multi-port smart balance chargers (SkyRC T1000 / ISDT K4 class, per doctrine) on steel racking; each pack charges in an individual steel/ceramic tray; LiPo-sack policy for any suspect pack |
| Electrical | Dedicated sub-board (Chapter 7 sizing); every rack circuit RCD-protected; master EPO mushroom at the door; a timed master contactor de-energizes all charge circuits outside staffed hours |
| Detection & suppression | Smoke + heat detection zoned to the park panel; no water sprinkler over lithium — Class D/ABC extinguishers at door plus a sand/vermiculite quench bin and lifting tongs; ventilation ≥ 6 air changes/hour extracting at high level **[verify locally]** |
| Monitoring | Temperature and smoke telemetry into RC WORLD OS; charger fleet on networked monitoring; CCTV inside (Chapter 13) |

> **Safety Warning** — The bunker's safety case rests on three assumptions that operations must never erode: (1) charging happens **only** in the bunker and the Chapter 7 customer charging station — never at pit bays, never in the battery room; (2) packs outside the 3.4–4.2 V/cell window or with any physical damage are quarantined in the sand bin, not racked; (3) the blow-out panels' exclusion strip stays fenced and empty — it is not storage. All three appear on the daily close-down checklist (Volume 7).

## 7. Pit Lane & Charging Station

Chapter 3.5 dimensioned the trackside working pit lane. This chapter is the *customer-facing* pit theatre and the park's second charging node — the operational heart of the Shift model, where every Operator Shift's battery swap (the "refueling" moment, canon) happens in public view, and where the park's highest continuous electrical load lives. Precinct: 450 m² (allocation line 6) between Track A and the guest spine.

### 7.1 Pit theatre layout

| Element | Dimension | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Swap counters | **8 counters, 1.5 m wide × 0.75 m deep** at 950 mm height, in a 12 m colonnade facing the guest spine | The stage: customer hands machine/transmitter over, Artisan swaps pack, RC WORLD OS logs the swap; over-counter task light and a lap-timer style swap clock per counter (theatre) |
| Transmitter racks | Two lockable racks, 48 slots each, behind the counters | Charged, sanitized, class-tagged transmitters; QR on each slot binds to vehicle at issue (Volume 3/OS doctrine) |
| Queue | Serpentine, 1.2 m lane width, capacity 40 guests, under a full shade canopy, with the swap counters and Track A both visible from every point in the queue | Watching swaps *is* the queue entertainment; live queue state feeds the app's `queue_roster` (canon) |
| Staff spine | 2.0 m corridor behind counters connecting to the trackside pit lane and the charging room | Fleet and packs move behind, never through, guests |
| Buffer racking | Vehicle staging racks for 30 machines | The ready line for the next Shifts |

### 7.2 Charging station equipment room

A 30 m² masonry room at the pit building's north end, built to the same doctrine as the Works bunker (fully filled CMU, FD90 door, blow-out panel to a fenced service strip, no sprinkler over lithium, EPO at door): the park's second bunker in all but name. Equipment: 10 multi-port smart balance chargers (T1000/K4 class), each serving 4 channels, on two steel racks with per-pack trays; storage racking for 200 packs in rotation; pack-triage bench with cell checker and IR meter.

### 7.3 Electrical load — worked example

Circuit sizing for the charging room, as a worked example the MEP engineer scales for the Works bunker (this method, with local code factors, is the deliverable — the numbers are the reference case) **[verify locally]**:

1. **Pack energy.** Reference pack: 2S 7.4 V nominal × 5 Ah = **37 Wh** (3S 11.1 V × 5 Ah = 55.5 Wh). Fleet mix ≈ 70/30 2S/3S → weighted ≈ 42.6 Wh/pack.
2. **Charge power per channel.** Doctrine charge rate 1C (5 A) at the 4.2 V/cell termination voltage with charger losses (η ≈ 0.85): 2S channel ≈ (8.4 V × 5 A)/0.85 ≈ **49 W**; 3S ≈ (12.6 × 5)/0.85 ≈ **74 W**. Weighted ≈ 57 W/channel.
3. **Connected load.** 10 chargers × 4 channels × 57 W ≈ **2.3 kW** charging + charger overhead/fans ≈ 0.3 kW + room services (lighting, extract fan, monitoring) ≈ 0.8 kW → **≈ 3.4 kW connected**.
4. **Demand.** All channels genuinely run together at peak turnover (diversity 1.0 on charge circuits — never diversify a battery room), room services diversity 0.8 → **design demand ≈ 3.2 kW ≈ 3.5 kVA at PF 0.95**. Note the packs arrive ~70% depleted at most (the canonical ~30% buffer returns with every Casual Shift), so the 1C session runs ≈ 50 minutes including the CV tail — the number step 6 uses.
5. **Circuits.** Two 20 A radial circuits per rack (5 chargers/rack, ≤ 1.5 kW/circuit — 50% loaded, cool and expandable), one 16 A services circuit, all 30 mA RCD-protected; sub-board 3-phase 32 A/phase with 40% spare ways. The Works bunker, with ~2.5× the channel count for the 450-pack fleet rotation, scales to ≈ 9 kVA by the same method.
6. **Throughput check.** 40 channels × ~50 min/pack ⇒ ≈ 48 packs/hour through the customer station — comfortably ahead of peak swap demand (8 counters × ~2 swaps/counter/Shift-block ≈ 48 packs/hour at full house), which is the point: the electrical design and the Shift model are the same calculation.

### 7.4 Fire suppression & controls

As §6.2: detection zoned to the park panel; extinguishers (ABC + Class D capability) both sides of the door; sand quench bin and tongs; thermal camera watchpoint over the racks feeding an RC WORLD OS alert; timed master contactor kills all charge power 30 minutes after close; the counters' public side needs nothing special — no pack is ever charged, opened or stored on the customer side of the wall. Signage: "LiPo CHARGING — AUTHORIZED STAFF ONLY", door held shut, never wedged.

## 8. Guest Buildings

### 8.1 Entry pavilion

The entry pavilion is the park's front door, wallet and classroom: **490 m² GFA**, single storey, steel frame with corten and glazed facades, fronting the arrival plaza at the guest gateway. Everything a guest must do before their first Shift — ticket, waiver, Toolbox Talk, transmitter familiarization — happens here, so the building is sized for the peak arrival pulse, not the daily average.

| Room | Area (m²) | Specification |
|---|---|---|
| Entrance hall & queue | 90 | 4 POS positions + 4 self-service kiosks (RC WORLD OS bookings/wallet); queue capacity 60 inside + 60 under plaza canopy; gate line with QR scan |
| Retail | **120** | Park-branded and hobby retail (Volume 9 owns range); 2 POS, lockable after-hours shutter to the hall so retail trades on event nights independently |
| **Briefing room (Toolbox Talk)** | 60 | 40 seats, projection wall, transmitter demo bench; the digital Toolbox Talk induction (canon) is completed in-app, but first-timers and groups get the live version here; doubles as party/school room off-peak |
| F&B kiosk | 35 | Phase 1 catering: counter service, coffee, packaged food; 3-phase supply and extract stub sized for a future fit-out upgrade |
| Guest toilets | 70 | Sized to peak-day load (§8.3): indicative 6 F + 4 M + urinals + 2 accessible + **2 family rooms** with change tables **[verify locally — fixture counts are code-driven]** |
| First-aid room | 12 | Per Chapter 13; street-accessible for ambulance handover |
| Staff & back-of-house | 45 | Cash office (Volume 10 controls), comms cabinet, cleaners' store, retail stock |
| Circulation & walls | 58 | — |
| **Total** | **490** | |

The plaza (part of precinct 1) carries the corten RC WORLD gateway totem, the park map, shade trees, and the "first machine in 60 seconds" sight line: from the gate line, guests see straight up the spine to Track A's main straight.

**Sizing check against the arrival pulse.** The pavilion is sized by the worst 30 minutes, not the day: on a Phase 1 peak day (~280 visitors), booking data from comparable timed-entry venues puts ~45% of arrivals inside one 30-minute pulse ≈ 126 guests. At 4 staffed POS × 90 s per group of 2.8 plus 4 kiosks × 60 s, gate throughput ≈ 300 persons/30 min — the pulse clears with half the positions down. The queue reservoir (60 inside + 60 canopy) holds the pulse entirely even at half throughput, which is the real design case (one trainee on POS, one kiosk faulted, it is raining). The briefing room's 40 seats turn over on the 20-minute Shift clock by design: a Toolbox Talk cohort empties into the park exactly as the next Shift block opens, so first-timers arrive at the pit theatre in phase with the operating rhythm rather than against it.

### 8.2 Restaurant (Phase 2)

A 380 m² GFA pavilion with its long glazed side and terrace overlooking Track A's T5 sweeper and main straight — the table with a view of the racing is the product.

### 8.3 Sanitary provision sized to peak load

Design population (Volume 2 demand model): Phase 1 design-day ≈ 140 simultaneous guests + 25 staff; Phase 2 ≈ 220 + 35; Phase 3 events ≈ 400. Provision strategy: the pavilion carries the Phase 1 load entirely; the restaurant block and a plumbed toilet pod at the grandstand carry Phase 2 growth; the arena carries its own event load. Family rooms (2 in the pavilion, 1 at the grandstand pod) reflect the park's family skew — stroller-parking bays beside every toilet block. All counts above are indicative for space-planning: **final fixture schedules come from the governing sanitary code applied to these populations [verify locally]**.

## 9. Viewing Areas & Circulation

### 9.1 Spectating as designed program

Roughly one companion watches for every driver on-station (Volume 2's visit-group data), so at Phase 2 design-day the park holds ~110 spectators who are the marketing department's unpaid film crew. The hierarchy:

| Viewing asset | Phase | Capacity | Specification |
|---|---|---|---|
| Grandstand at Track A | 2 | **200 seated** | 5 tiers × 40; steel frame, timber seats, 400 mm row rise / 800 mm going (C-value sight-line check over a standing child at the rail — RC spectating looks *down*, so generous rise matters more than at a stadium); full shade canopy; front row +1.2 m above track datum behind the two-stage barrier; accessible platform for 6 wheelchairs + companions at tier 1 **[verify locally]** |
| Elevated mining walkway | 1 | 60 standing | **1.8 m wide × 30 m long at +2.4 m** above pit datum, crossing the Mining Zone's west end; steel structure, mesh balustrade **1.3 m** with kick-plate (elevated = taller rail), anti-drop mesh to 100 mm aperture full height — nothing droppable reaches the pit; ramped access 1:14 both ends; the park's signature photo spot, looking down the haul-road loop to the hopper |
| Viewing mounds (berm tops) | 1 | ~150 standing total | The Chapter 11 berms double as terraced viewing: sleeper-edged terraces cut into the south faces at Track B and the airfield promenade |
| Spectator terraces | 1 | continuous | The 2 m terrace behind mining's operator line (Volume 4), Track C boardwalk widenings, pond spectator quay (Volume 6: 12 × 4 m canopy, 30 spectators) |
| Airfield promenade | 2 | 80 standing | 60 × 6 m along the cage's south face, fine-mesh spectator panel + 25 mm skirt net (Volume 5), lean rail, interpretive graphics |

### 9.2 Circulation network

- **Main spine:** 3.0 m compacted stone with concrete bands at building thresholds, entry plaza → Track A/pit theatre → mining/agriculture junction → northern zones. 3.0 m passes two strollers plus a counter-flow group and admits the smaller utility vehicle for out-of-hours service.
- **Secondary loops:** 2.0 m paths to each zone's viewing edge; 1.8 m boardwalk in Track C; all gradients ≤ 1:20 preferred, 1:14 max with landings **[verify locally]** for accessibility code.
- **One-way flow at peak:** the spine and the mining walkway are the two pinch candidates. At >150 guests on site (RC WORLD OS occupancy counter), duty management activates the posted one-way scheme: spine flows clockwise (north on the west side, south on the east), the mining walkway becomes west→east one-way, and the grandstand stair pair splits up/down. The scheme is signed with flip-panels at five decision points — no temporary barriers needed.
- **Capacity check:** at the leisure-comfortable planning rate of ~25 persons/min per metre of clear path width (well below crush thresholds — this is a strolling park, not a stadium concourse), the 3.0 m spine passes ≈ 75 persons/min two-way and roughly the same one-way with the counter-flow removed; the whole Phase 2 design-day population could traverse it in under four minutes. The binding constraint is never the path — it is *stationary* people: a crowd three deep at Track A's barrier narrows the adjacent spine to 1.2 m. Hence the standing rule for detailed design: **every barrier where crowds predictably form gets a 2 m spectator layby off the path edge** (built as paving band, drawn on the layout plans), so watchers stand out of the stream. The mining walkway (1.8 m) is capacity-managed instead: a marshal-clicked or camera-counted cap of 60, queue at the west ramp, one-way at peak.
- **Queue capacities (designed, not residual):** pit theatre 40 (§7.1); entry 120 (§8.1); mining operator wait 24 under the rim sails; airfield vestibule 12; restaurant wait 20 on terrace stair. Every queue has shade, sight of the action, and a posted "next Shift" screen fed by RC WORLD OS.

### 9.3 Wayfinding and themed naming

One family of corten totems (1.8 m blade, laser-cut lettering, zone pictogram, painted interior faces in zone colours) at every decision point; fingerposts at path junctions; zone gateways as scaffold-and-corten portals with the zone name in DIN stencil. Naming is industrial-diegetic and consistent across map, app and signage — the park reads as a worksite you've been badged into:

| Asset | Public name |
|---|---|
| Main spine | **The Haul Road** |

## 10. Parking & Access

### 10.1 Demand model and bay counts

From Volume 2's peak-day model (≈ 220–300 visitors on Phase 1 peaks, ~400 at Phase 2 events): average vehicle occupancy 2.8 (family skew), ~78% arriving by car, dwell 3.5 h with two arrival pulses. Required peak accumulation ≈ 84 cars (Phase 1) / 122 (Phase 2 event day).

| Bay type | Phase 1 | Phase 2 build-out | Dimensions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard car | 80 | 120 | 2.5 × 5.0 m, aisles 6.0 m, 90° |
| Accessible | 5 | 8 | 3.6 × 5.0 m adjacent to plaza, level route **[verify locally — ratio is code-driven]** |
| Family priority | 3 | 4 | 3.2 × 5.0 m, next band out from accessible |
| Coach/bus | 2 | 4 | 3.5 × 15 m, drive-through — school coaches never reverse |
| Motorcycle/cycle | 10 + 20 racks | 16 + 30 | at the plaza edge, covered cycle racks |
| **Total car bays** | **88** | **132** | surface, permeable gravel-grid on the outer bands (Chapter 11) |

**Worked accumulation model (Phase 1 peak day, 280 visitors).** Arrivals split across two pulses (10:00–11:30 ≈ 55%, 13:00–14:30 ≈ 35%, trickle 10%); car share 78% at 2.8 occupancy ⇒ 78 cars/day. With 3.5 h mean dwell, peak accumulation occurs ≈ 13:30 when the morning pulse has not yet fully departed: accumulation = (0.55 × 78 × 0.85 retained) + (0.35 × 78 × 0.60 arrived) ≈ 36 + 16 ≈ **53 cars typical peak, 84 at the 95th-percentile day** (longer dwell + event overlay). Phase 1's 88 bays therefore run at ≈ 60% typical / ≈ 95% design-day — full is acceptable twice a month, queuing onto the public road is never acceptable, hence the drop-off loop is outside the parking circulation (a full car park must not block drop-off) and the L2 overflow protocol below exists from day one. The same model at Phase 2 event days (400 visitors, 4.5 h dwell) yields ≈ 122 cars against 132 bays. These coefficients (car share, occupancy, dwell, pulse shape) are restated as a live tab in Volume 10's model — re-run them with real RC WORLD OS visit data at Month 6 and let the Phase 2 parking extension be sized by evidence, not by this page.

Overflow for Phase 3 events: the land-bank parcel L2 (Chapter 14) is graded and gated as marshalled grass overflow (~80 cars) before any permanent expansion is considered.

### 10.2 Drop-off and access geometry

- **Drop-off loop:** one-way counterclockwise loop off the frontage at the plaza, 6.0 m lane, 5 pull-in bays + 1 accessible, no parking, 2-minute rule signed; coach drop-off on the loop's outer edge with a 20 m level footway to the gate.
- **Guest access:** single signalized/priority junction per highway authority requirements **[verify locally]**; sight-distance splays kept clear in the landscape plan.
- **Service route:** a separate gated entry 90 m east of the guest junction feeds the eastern service road directly to The Works' yard, the airfield gate and the arena dock — **delivery vehicles never enter guest circulation**. Design vehicle: 12 m rigid truck (net poles and pond liner arrive on articulated vehicles twice ever — those movements are managed deliveries on closed days).
- **Emergency access:** two fire-appliance routes — the frontage/plaza and the eastern service road — plus the northern staff route (§4.3) giving a 4.5 m-wide hard route to within 45 m of every structure; gates on the emergency routes take the local brigade padlock/key system **[verify locally]**.

## 11. Landscaping & Environment

### 11.1 Berms: noise control that sells tickets

The park's earthworks balance goes into perimeter berms — spoil from the pond, pit and track excavations becomes the landscape (target: zero soil export):

| Berm | Location | Profile | Functions |
|---|---|---|---|
| North berm | Full northern boundary, ~180 m | h = 3.0 m, crest 2 m wide, guest face 1:3, boundary face 1:2 | Acoustic screen for the loud band (mining, Track B, airfield); wind shelter; terraced viewing on the south face at Track B |
| West berm | West boundary at the pond, ~90 m | h = 3.0 m + 2 m evergreen hedge on crest | The marine wind shelter Volume 6 prices as revenue; afternoon shade for Agriculture |
| Frontage berm | South, broken at gates | h = 1.5 m, planted | Visual dress to the road; keeps the cage and gateway visible above it by design |

Acoustic performance to be verified by the consultant against the Chapter 2.3 targets **[verify locally]**; as a planning rule of thumb a 3 m berm breaking line-of-sight yields ~5–8 dB attenuation at the boundary — the gradient plan does the rest.

### 11.2 Planting palette

Three rules govern species selection (local ecologist adapts the list **[verify locally]**): drought-tolerant once established (irrigation is for turf and hedges only), no thorn species within reach of guest paths, and — critically — **low-FOD near the airfield**: within 30 m of the cage, no species that sheds cones, large seed pods, catkins or twiggy debris that ends up on the runway or in the nets. Evergreen, small-leaf, deep-rooting species (holm-oak/olive/pittosporum types in temperate-dry climates) around the cage; deciduous shade trees are welcome at the plaza, restaurant and southern spine where their leaf-fall lands on sweepable paving; ornamental grasses and gravel-garden planting dress the berms (industrial-authentic: the palette of a rehabilitated quarry, not a resort).

### 11.3 Dust suppression

Dust is the operating cost of a dirt park: Track B's watering ring (§3.2), mining's nightly wet-grooming (Volume 4), the northern service road dressed in crusher fines with a calcium-chloride/lignin binder refreshed each season, and hose points at 40 m spacing on the irrigation main. Wind-blown dust from the loose zones is intercepted by the berm-and-hedge line before it reaches the pond (skimmer load) or the airfield (runway grip). The morning "hose-and-broom reset" (design tenet 4, §1.2) is a designed capability: every zone has a washdown point, falls, and a silt trap.

### 11.4 Stormwater and drainage strategy

The 2–4% SW grade organizes the whole strategy: a network of grass swales along the path edges collects zone runoff (each zone discharging through its own silt trap — mining's fines and Track B's clay never reach the network raw) and feeds the **SW detention basin** (~600 m³, side slopes 1:4, max design depth 600 mm, dry between storms, planted as a rain garden) which throttles discharge to the municipal system or watercourse at the permitted rate **[verify locally]**. Hard-surface ratio at build-out ≈ 31% (Chapter 2.1); car-park outer bands in permeable grid pavers reduce the peak. The pond is hydraulically independent (lined, top-up metered); its overflow weir discharges to the swale network. Design storm and discharge consent are jurisdictional **[verify locally]** — the layout reserves the basin footprint for the wettest plausible case.

### 11.5 Shade strategy

Shade is a throughput input: dwell collapses on unshaded summer sites. Layered provision — engineered sails over every operator station, rostrum and queue (§§3–7); canopy trees at plaza, lawn and spine seating; built canopies at grandstand and spectator quay; and the buildings' own deep eaves on southern facades. Target: at 14:00 on the summer design day, **≥ 60% of all designed guest positions (stations, seats, queues) are in shade**. Sails come down for the storm season per the maintenance calendar (wind rating on every sail post is a structural item **[verify locally]**).

## 12. Utilities & Infrastructure

### 12.1 Electrical: single-line concept

The park takes a municipal three-phase LV supply at the frontage (upgradeable connection ≥ 200 kVA — a site-selection ● item). Concept single line:

```
  MUNICIPAL LV SUPPLY (3-ph, ≥200 kVA capacity)
        │
   ┌────┴─────┐  metering + main switch
   │  MAIN    │  MB-01, entry pavilion plant room
   │  BOARD   │
   └─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │ │ │ │ │                                                │
     │ │ │ │ └─▶ SB-ENT entry pavilion / retail / F&B kiosk   │ ESSENTIAL BUS
     │ │ │ └───▶ SB-WKS The Works (incl. bunker sub-board)    │  ┌──────────┐
     │ │ └─────▶ SB-PIT pit theatre + charging station        ├──┤ 40 kVA   │
     │ └───────▶ SB-MSP motorsport (tracks, rostrum, timing)  │  │GENERATOR │
     └─────────▶ SB-CON construction + agriculture zones      │  │ + UPS    │
        Phase 2: SB-AVN airfield · SB-MAR marine + plant      │  │ (comms/  │
                 SB-RST restaurant                            │  │  OS/CCTV)│
        Phase 3: SB-ARN arena · SB-LTG night-race lighting    │  └──────────┘
  Essential bus carries: comms room, RC WORLD OS servers/network, CCTV,
  safety PA, zone kill-switch infrastructure, marine circulation pumps,
  emergency lighting. Generator auto-start; UPS bridges the start gap.
```

Design intents the MEP engineer must preserve: each zone's sub-board is *in* its zone (fault isolation per zone; a track fault never darkens the pit); both charging rooms are separately metered sub-boards with timed master contactors (§6.2, §7.4); the essential bus keeps **RC WORLD OS, the network, CCTV, PA and the telemetry kill-switch chain alive through any supply event** — the safety system's power is never hostage to the park's; and every sub-board carries ≥ 30% spare ways (this park adds circuits every season of its life).

### 12.2 Site-wide load schedule

| Board | Serves | Connected (kVA) | Demand est. (kVA) | Phase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SB-ENT | Pavilion, retail, F&B kiosk, plaza | 40 | 28 | 1 |
| SB-WKS | The Works incl. bunker (≈ 9) + compressor | 45 | 30 | 1 |
| SB-PIT | Pit theatre + charging station (≈ 3.5) | 12 | 8 | 1 |
| SB-MSP | Tracks A/B/C: timing, PA, rostrum power, watering pump | 15 | 8 | 1 |
| SB-CON | Mining (hopper, conveyor) + agriculture + service route | 12 | 7 | 1 |
| **Phase 1 total** | | **124** | **≈ 81** | |
| SB-AVN | Airfield: gate interlocks, PA, flight-line container, promenade | 8 | 5 | 2 |
| SB-MAR | Marine plant (pumps, UV), marina, quay | 18 | 12 | 2 |
| SB-RST | Restaurant kitchen + dining | 60 | 38 | 2 |
| **Phase 2 total** | | **210** | **≈ 136** | |
| SB-ARN | Arena, academy, corporate centre | 80 | 45 | 3 |
| SB-LTG | Night-racing floodlighting (Tracks A+B) | 30 | 26 | 3 |
| **Phase 3 total** | | **320** | **≈ 207** | |

The Phase 1 connection is sized for Phase 2 (≈ 140 kVA demand); the Phase 3 step (arena + lighting) triggers the connection upgrade priced in Volume 10's Phase 3 capex. Diversity assumptions above are planning-grade; the MEP engineer recalculates to the local method **[verify locally]**.

### 12.3 Water

- **Mains:** municipal potable connection at the frontage; meter + backflow prevention **[verify locally]**; potable distribution to pavilion, Works, restaurant, first-aid, hose-union points.
- **Pond top-up:** metered branch with air-gap break tank at the marine plant room (§5.5); budget evaporation + splash losses ≈ 1–2% of volume/week in summer (≈ 7–13 m³/week) — the meter reading is a Volume 6 weekly checklist item.
- **Irrigation & dust suppression:** a dedicated non-potable ring main (fed from mains in Phase 1; a rainwater-harvest tank at The Works' roof is the Phase 2 upgrade) serving Track B's watering ring, the hose points at 40 m spacing, hedge drip lines and the turf overruns.
- **Sewer:** pavilion, Works and restaurant to the municipal sewer (or approved on-site treatment — site-selection item); kitchen via grease interceptor; workshop intake sink via silt/oil interceptor; pond backwash to sewer, never to the swales **[verify locally]**.

### 12.4 Data: the park is a radio site

RC WORLD OS and the telemetry chain make connectivity a life-safety utility (the kill-switch rides on it — canon). Per source doctrine: a **TP-Link Omada-class outdoor Wi-Fi mesh** blankets the park so ESP32 2.4 GHz Nodes hand off between APs without dropping telemetry.

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Comms room | Rack cabinet in The Works' electronics lab (§6.3): router/firewall, PoE switches, OS edge server, UPS (essential bus); a second distribution cabinet at the entry pavilion |
| AP plan | **12 outdoor PoE APs Phase 1** on 4–6 m poles or building facades: 2 × Track A, 1 × Track B, 1 × Track C, 2 × Mining (rim + hopper), 1 × Agriculture, 2 × pit/spine, 1 × plaza, 2 × The Works/yard. Phase 2 adds 5 (cage corners ×2, promenade, marina, restaurant); Phase 3 adds arena indoor set. Design target: **−65 dBm or better at machine height (0.3 m) over 100% of operating surfaces**, validated by a post-build survey at machine height, not head height |
| Backbone | Single-mode fibre in a 100 mm duct ring following the spine and service road, drawn at Phase 1 full-length (including Phase 2/3 stubs); APs on Cat6A from zone poles |
| Segregation | Three SSIDs/VLANs: telemetry+ops (Nodes, kill-switch, timing), staff (OS clients, POS, CCTV), guest (captive portal); telemetry VLAN has priority QoS — a full guest Wi-Fi never delays a KILL command |
| Resilience | Comms room + all APs' PoE switches on the essential bus; 4G/5G failover router for payments and OS cloud sync |

**Duct schedule (Phase 1 civils — the cheapest insurance in the project):**

| Route | Ducts | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| Frontage → pavilion plant room | 2 × 100 + 2 × 50 mm | Incoming supply, incoming telecom, spares |
| Pavilion → The Works (spine route) | 2 × 100 + 4 × 50 mm | Fibre ring leg, LV interlink, CCTV/PA, spares |
| The Works → airfield parcel (service road) | 2 × 100 + 2 × 50 mm | Phase 2 SB-AVN feed, fibre, cage systems |
| Spine → marine parcel | 2 × 100 + 2 × 50 mm | Phase 2 SB-MAR feed, plant controls, fibre |
| Track A perimeter ring | 2 × 50 mm + loop conduits | Timing, cameras, Phase 3 floodlighting |
| Spine → arena parcel (SE) | 2 × 100 + 2 × 50 mm | Phase 3 SB-ARN feed, fibre |
| Zone pole positions (all) | 1 × 50 mm each from nearest chamber | AP + CCTV + PA co-mounted per pole |

Draw pits at ≤ 50 m spacing and every change of direction; every duct proved and roped at handover (checklist item). The rule stated once and enforced always: **ducts now, trenches never** — no open-cut through a live park is ever approved for a service that this schedule could have carried.

### 12.5 Lighting

- **Operational (Phase 1):** path and plaza lighting to 20 lux average (guest areas after dusk), building task lighting per §6.3, statutory emergency lighting **[verify locally]**. Zones are daylight operations in Phase 1 — zone lighting is close-down/security level only.
- **Night racing (Phase 3, SB-LTG):** Track A floodlit to **300 lux maintained average on the racing line, uniformity ≥ 0.5** (Volume 3's interface figure, uprated from event experience if league TV coverage demands), Track B to 200 lux; 8–10 m poles with full-cutoff LED floods aimed by a lighting designer to keep obtrusive spill below curfew limits at the boundary **[verify locally]** and — a park-specific constraint — **no fitting within the drivers' rostrum sight cone may be aimed toward the rostrum** (glare on a driver is a crash). Conduit and pole bases are cast in at Phase 1 track construction (Chapter 2.4 doctrine: ducts now, trenches never).

## 13. Security & Safety Systems

### 13.1 Perimeter and fencing

| Line | Specification |
|---|---|
| Site perimeter | 1.8 m galvanized weldmesh (358-class anti-climb on the road frontage and service gates), concealed in the berm/hedge line where it crosses guest views |
| Zone edges (guest/live separation) | The 1.1 m rail-and-kick-plate family (§1.1); mesh infill ≤ 100 mm aperture wherever small children queue |
| Pond precinct | 1.1 m with self-closing self-latching gates (Volume 6 canon) **[verify locally]** |
| Charging rooms, plant, bunker strips | 2.0 m mesh enclosures, locked, signed |
| Construction phase lines | 2.0 m temporary hoarding, graphics-wrapped (the hoarding sells Phase 2) |

### 13.2 CCTV coverage logic

Coverage is designed by *incident question*, not camera count — every location where the operation would ask "what happened?" gets a view: all POS and cash handling; both charging rooms (interior, thermal watchpoint per §7.4); every zone's operating surface (the same masts as the Wi-Fi APs — one pole family carries AP + camera + PA horn); all gates and interlocks; the pond waterline (two views, full surface); the car park and drop-off; The Works' intake (asset chain-of-custody). Phase 1 ≈ 32 cameras, PoE, recorded 30 days at the comms room NVR (essential bus), with RC WORLD OS integration limited to event bookmarks (a kill-switch trigger or gate alarm bookmarks the relevant streams). Privacy signage and retention per local law **[verify locally]**.

| Coverage group | Cameras (Ph. 1) | View standard |
|---|---|---|
| POS / cash office / retail | 6 | Identify (face-recognizable at counter) |
| Charging rooms + battery room | 4 + 2 thermal watchpoints | Detect + thermal alarm |
| Zone operating surfaces (Tracks A/B/C, mining, agriculture) | 10 | Observe (incident reconstruction, machine-scale) |
| Gates, interlocks, service road | 5 | Recognize (badge-holder at gate) |
| Car park, drop-off, plaza | 5 | Observe + plate capture at both vehicle gates |
| The Works intake & yard | 2 | Recognize (asset chain-of-custody) |

Phase 2 adds ≈ 10 (pond waterline ×2, marina, cage interior ×2, promenade, restaurant, grandstand, events lawn, extension parking); Phase 3 the arena interior set. One deliberate omission: no camera is pointed at the rostrum drivers' faces at eye level — telemetry already records what their vehicles did, and the park photographs its guests for joy (Volume 9's media program), not surveillance.

### 13.3 Access control tied to RC WORLD OS roles

Physical access mirrors the OS role model (canon: executive, finance, HR, operations, artisan/technician, marshal, front-of-house, franchisee, customer): staff badges (RFID + QR fallback) open what the role's OS permissions imply, and nothing else.

| Access zone | Roles admitted |
|---|---|
| Guest areas | All (customers via ticket QR at the gate line) |
| Trackside pit lane, zone service edges | Marshal, Artisan, Operations, Executive |
| The Works (except bunker) | Artisan, Operations, Executive |
| **Charging bunker & charging station room** | Artisan (charging-trained flag in OS) + Operations only; door controller checks the training flag |
| Comms room, cash office | Named individuals; dual-badge for the cash office (Volume 10 controls) |
| Interlocked live-zone gates | Marshal badge + zone status "safe" in OS — the gate is the physical face of the software interlock |

### 13.4 Emergency preparedness

- **First-aid points:** the pavilion first-aid room (§8.1, ambulance-accessible) plus wall stations (AED, trauma kit, burn kit) at the pit theatre, The Works and — Phase 2 — the marina. Burn kits acknowledge the LiPo risk profile.
- **Assembly points:** two — the events lawn (north assembly) and the car-park head (south assembly), signed from every zone; choice of two means no route past a plausible incident (fire at The Works blocks neither).
- **PA:** zone horns on the AP/CCTV poles, addressable by zone from the duty office and the OS duty console; the all-park evacuation tone is generator-backed.
- **Lightning protection:** the airfield's 17 m poles are the site's air terminals whether planned or not — so plan it: the cage poles are bonded and earthed as a lightning protection system by the electrical designer **[verify locally]**, the flight program's storm rules (Volume 5) close the cage well before risk, and the same weather trigger closes the pond (Volume 6) and clears the mining rim's sail line. A site lightning-risk assessment is a Phase 2 design deliverable.
- **Fire zones and extinguisher schedule:** the site is zoned to the detection panel as: Z1 pavilion/retail, Z2 The Works, **Z2B bunker**, Z3 pit/charging, Z4 restaurant (Ph. 2), Z5 arena (Ph. 3), plus external plant nodes. Extinguisher family **[verify locally — types/spacing are code items]**: ABC dry powder at all plant and vehicles; CO₂ at electrical boards and comms; wet chemical at kitchens; **Class D capability + sand quench bins at both charging rooms and the battery room**; travel distance to an extinguisher ≤ 20 m back-of-house.

> **Safety Warning** — The interlock chain (OS zone status → gate release → marshal badge) is only as safe as its failure mode. Specify every live-zone gate **fail-secure for entry, fail-safe for exit**: a network or power failure must never trap a person inside a zone, and must never release public entry into one. This requirement is written on the door-hardware schedule, tested at commissioning, and re-tested quarterly (Volume 7 maintenance matrix).

## 14. Future Expansion

### 14.1 Phase 3 indoor arena

The arena makes RC WORLD weather-proof and books-corporate: a clear-span portal-frame hall on the SE parcel, fronting the service road and frontage so events traffic never enters the park.

| Parameter | Specification |
|---|---|
| Clear span | **40 × 25 m (1,000 m²) column-free**, 7 m clear under haunches — reconfigurable indoor track (carpet/asphalt-tile modular), drone micro-cage, or 600-seat corporate floor |
| Total GFA | 1,600 m²: arena + 2 RC Academy classrooms (60 m² each, 16 students — Volume 9's curriculum), corporate suite (150 m² divisible, catering pantry served from the restaurant kitchen), stores, WCs, plant |
| Floor | Power-floated slab, 5 kPa, cast-in timing-loop conduit grid at 5 m centers (any layout finds a loop) |
| Services | SB-ARN (Ch. 12); its own entrance plaza and 20-bay evening parking overlay |
| Interface | A gated link path to the park spine — arena events can buy park access as an upsell, but default to self-contained |

### 14.2 Land-banking within the 4.8 ha

Two parcels (allocation line 19, 5,200 m² total) are held in low-cost landscape: **L1 (north-east, 2,800 m²)** beside the airfield — the natural home of a future cage extension, a second crawler landscape, or franchise-training compound; **L2 (south-east, 2,400 m²)** behind the arena — events overflow parking (§10.1) and the arena's expansion room. Both are graded, drained and duct-served at Phase 1 (the standing rule: ducts now, trenches never), planted as meadow, and protected by a one-line covenant in every future drawing issue: *no permanent structure on L1/L2 without a master-plan revision through this volume.*

### 14.3 Second-site learnings

Everything this volume fixes — the adjacency logic, the noise gradient, zone envelopes, the room schedules, the load schedule — is the *reference design* that Volume 12 turns into a franchise kit-of-parts: which dimensions are doctrine (haul-road 15°, pond 800 mm, cage envelope, bunker construction, sight-line rules), which are climate-adaptable (shade ratios, indoor-hybrid variants for Gulf and monsoon markets flagged in Volume 2), and which are free (track layout within the geometric rules, palette species, building expression). As-built deviations from this volume at the reference site must be logged in the drawing register *with reasons* — the second site inherits the reasons, not just the drawings. See Volume 12, Chapter 3.

## Handover checklist (design → construction → operations)

- [ ] Topographic + geotechnical surveys reconciled with the Chapter 2 allocation plan; setting-out grid issued.
- [ ] All **[verify locally]** items dispositioned in a code-compliance register signed by the local engineer of record.
- [ ] Hold-point dimensions verified on setting-out: haul-road grades ≤ 15° (built 14°), lane widths (agriculture 600 mm), pond depth ≤ 800 mm, cage envelope 60 × 40 × 15 m, jump landing ratio ≥ 5:1, rail heights 1.1 m / 1.3 m elevated.
- [ ] Cast-in items confirmed before pours: timing-loop conduits (Tracks A/B, arena grid), lighting pole bases and ducts, pond pipework, hopper holding-down bolts, duct ring with Phase 2/3 stubs.
- [ ] Charging bunker + charging station: construction per §6.2/§7.2 witnessed (filled CMU, blow-out panels, FD90 doors, EPO, contactor timing tested).
- [ ] Interlock chain commissioned: every live-zone gate tested fail-secure-in/fail-safe-out with OS zone status; results in the O&M file.
- [ ] Wi-Fi survey at machine height (0.3 m) shows ≥ −65 dBm on 100% of operating surfaces; kill-switch latency test passed park-wide.
- [ ] Net installation certified by the net engineer: pretension witness gauges recorded, ground-seal gap ≤ 50 mm full perimeter, panel lacing per spec.
- [ ] Rostrum and operator-station sight-line checks signed (every position sees its full envelope; Track A checked bidirectionally).
- [ ] Drainage proved: hose-test every zone to its silt trap; detention basin outlet at consented rate.
- [ ] As-built drawings, O&M manuals, and the deviations-with-reasons register lodged (feeds §14.3 and Volume 12).
- [ ] Signage and wayfinding snag-round scheduled for Month 2 post-opening (§9.3).

## Volume summary & cross-references

Volume 11 converts RC WORLD's operating doctrine into buildable geometry on the canonical 4.8 ha reference site. Its fixed decisions: a fully allocated **48,000 m² master plan** (Phase 1 60.4%, Phase 2 22.9%, Phase 3 + land bank 16.7%) organized by a south-to-north noise gradient with Mining beside The Works and the airfield peripheral-downwind; an **industrial-authentic** materials and naming language governed by the sight-line doctrine (*see everything, touch nothing live*, 1.1 m rail family, interlocked gates); **Track A** at ~180 m/3.5–4.5 m with a 58 m straight, 15 mm kerbs and two-stage barriers; **Track B** at ~160 m with 5:1 landing-ratio tabletops and 400 mm berms; a ten-feature **Track C** with 120 mm water-depth limits; the Volume 4 mining/agriculture geometry carried into civil detail (300 mm benches, 14° ramps, 4.0 m station pitch at 1.1 m rails); the Volume 5 cage (60 × 40 × 15 m) and Volume 6 basins (40 × 25 m at ≤ 800 mm) given their structures, liners and plant; a **450 m² Works** with a doctrine-compliant 30 m² charging bunker and a 490 m² entry pavilion with 120 m² retail; a worked charging-load method (≈ 3.5 kVA customer station, ≈ 9 kVA bunker); a site load schedule reaching ≈ 207 kVA demand at Phase 3; a 12-AP telemetry-grade Wi-Fi plan; and role-keyed access control that makes RC WORLD OS's permissions physical.

**Cross-references.** Volume 1 carries the master-plan summary for investors. Volume 2 supplies the demand model behind capacity, parking and catchment (Chapters 7) and the diorama-supplier channel behind zone dressing (Chapter 4). Volume 3 governs everything on wheels on Tracks A/B and the racing program this geometry serves (its Sections 9.6/10.4 are closed out by Chapter 3 here). Volume 4 is source of truth for Mining and Agriculture internals restated in Chapter 4. Volume 5 owns the cage rationale and netting spec built in Chapter 5; Volume 6 owns the waterspace doctrine behind §5.4–5.5. Volume 7 operates The Works designed in Chapter 6 and owns the maintenance regimes this fabric assumes. Volume 8 procures the materials, nets, chargers and dressing packages. Volume 9 programs the guest journey through Chapters 8–9's spaces. Volume 10 carries the capex these drawings imply and the phasing economics of Chapter 2.4. Volume 12 inherits the reference design per §14.3. Volume 13 specifies RC WORLD OS, whose zone statuses, roles and telemetry this volume wires into gates, screens and the essential bus.

# Volume 12 — Franchise Manual

**RC WORLD — Master Development Plan** · Volume 12 of 12
**Revision:** 1.0 · **Date:** July 2026 · **Status:** Living document — bump revision on material change

**Purpose of this volume.** This volume defines how the RC WORLD business is replicated: the franchise strategy and its rationale, the three licensed park formats, the international expansion framework, the legal and licensing architecture, the fee structure and unit economics for both franchisee and franchisor, and the complete operating machinery of a franchise system — recruitment, site approval, training through the RC WORLD Academy, brand standards, quality audits, and franchisor support operations. It is written *before* the first franchise is sold, deliberately: the founding thesis of this volume is that the thirteen-volume documented system you are holding — engineering specifications, SOPs, fleet doctrine, procurement channels, RCW Node hardware, RC WORLD OS software, and the customer-experience canon — **is the franchise product**. The flagship park proves it; this volume packages it. The franchise pilot is a Phase 3 activity (months 31–60); everything here is sequenced against that canon.

**Intended readers.** The founder and board; the Franchise Director hired in Phase 3; investors and lenders evaluating the long-term equity story beyond a single park; prospective franchisees and master franchisees conducting due diligence; legal counsel preparing disclosure documents; the RC WORLD OS team building multi-site capability (Volume 13).

**Chapters**

1. Franchise Strategy & Rationale
2. Franchise Models & Formats
3. International Expansion Strategy

> **Legal framing for the entire volume.** Franchising is one of the most heavily regulated commercial formats in the world, and the rules differ materially by country and, in federal systems, by state or province. Every legal mechanism described in this volume — disclosure documents, fee structures, termination rights, territory protections, non-competes — is a **design intention to be verified and implemented with qualified local franchise counsel** in each target jurisdiction before any offer is made. Nothing in this volume is legal advice, and no franchise may be offered on the basis of this document alone.

## 1. Franchise Strategy & Rationale

### 1.1 Why franchise at all

RC WORLD's flagship park is designed to reach roughly $3.4 M revenue by Year 5 at a 24–28% EBITDA margin (Volume 10). That is a good business, but it is one park. The strategic question for Phase 3 and beyond is how the concept scales, and there are only three honest answers: build more owned parks, franchise, or do nothing. This volume argues for a **flagship-plus-franchise** model, for four reasons.

**Capital efficiency.** A full park consumes ≈ $3.9 M of capex over five years and ≈ $2.6 M of external funding (canonical figures, Volume 10). Owned expansion at three parks means raising and risking roughly $8 M of additional capital while management attention is split across construction projects in different cities. Franchising moves the site capex onto the franchisee's balance sheet and converts RC WORLD's growth into a royalty and technology-fee stream that carries software-like margins once the support organization exists.

**The product is already written down.** Most first-time franchisors fail at the same hurdle: the founder's business runs on tacit knowledge that was never documented, so the "system" being sold does not actually exist in transferable form. RC WORLD inverts this. The Master Development Plan was commissioned from day one as an investor prospectus, operations manual, and engineering handbook. Fleet balancing methodology (Volume 3), the excavator-to-dump-truck 1:3 ratio and haul-road doctrine (Volume 4), workshop rebuild procedures and trade hacks (Volume 7), the procurement network with named suppliers and landed-cost models (Volume 8), the RC WORLD License progression (Volume 9), the financial model (Volume 10), the park design standards (Volume 11), and the RC WORLD OS platform with role-based interfaces including a dedicated **franchisee role** (Volume 13) — these are the deliverables a franchisee is paying for. The license fee buys access to a documented, versioned, living system, not a handshake and a logo.

**Hard-to-copy assets travel well.** The defensible core of RC WORLD is not the land or the buildings — any competitor can lease a field. It is (a) the RCW Node telemetry hardware and kill-switch architecture, (b) RC WORLD OS and its operational data, (c) the wholesale procurement relationships built in Volume 8, (d) the engineering doctrine that keeps a rental fleet of ~150 powered assets at high availability, and (e) the customer-experience mechanics — Toolbox Talk, the Shift, the Tow-Truck Retrieval Protocol, the License system. All five are *portable*: they cost the franchisor almost nothing to deliver to a second site, and they are exactly the things a would-be imitator cannot buy off a shelf.

**Local knowledge is genuinely local.** An RC park lives or dies on land acquisition, municipal relationships, local marketing, school and corporate networks, and weekend labor markets. A franchisee who owns those relationships in Kuala Lumpur or Dubai will outperform a head-office expatriate manager, and their own capital at risk aligns incentives in a way salaries never do.

### 1.2 What is genuinely replicable — and what is not

Franchise systems fail when they license things that do not transfer. The table below is the honest inventory, and it drives everything in Chapters 2 and 4.

| Asset | Replicable? | Transfer mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Park layout & civil design standards | Yes | Volume 11 design standards + franchisor design review gates (Chapter 7) |
| Fleet doctrine, models, ratios (1:3, 3:1 batteries, class ladder) | Yes | Volumes 3–6 + approved-equipment list, updated quarterly |
| Workshop practices, spares strategy, rebuild skills | Yes, with training | Volume 7 + Artisan certification at the flagship (Chapter 8) |
| Procurement channel (wholesale China network) | Yes | Central procurement desk (Chapter 11); Volume 8 as reference |
| RCW Node hardware & kill-switch logic | Yes, controlled | Nodes supplied only by franchisor; firmware signed; no design transfer |
| RC WORLD OS | Yes | SaaS license, multi-site tenancy (Volume 13, Chapter on franchise support) |
| Customer-experience canon (Toolbox Talk, Shift, Tow-Truck Retrieval Protocol, License, Gears) | Yes | Brand standards (Chapter 9) + OS enforcement |
| Brand & trademarks | Yes | License grant (Chapter 4) |
| Flagship's specific land economics & city demographics | **No** | Site criteria + local adaptation, never copied blindly |
| Founder's personal network & improvisation | **No** | Must be replaced by documentation and the Academy — this is the test of the whole plan |

### 1.3 The flagship-first proof requirement

RC WORLD will not sell a franchise on projections. The self-imposed, non-negotiable gate is:

> **No franchise will be offered until the flagship park has a minimum of two full years of operating data**, including at least one complete seasonal cycle at Full Park scope (Phase 2), audited financials demonstrating the unit economics claimed in disclosure materials, and a documented safety record.

Sequenced against the canonical phasing — Phase 1 (months 0–12) builds the Core Park, Phase 2 (months 13–30) completes the Full Park, Phase 3 (months 31–60) includes the franchise pilot — this means the earliest a franchise agreement is *signed* is around month 36, and the pilot park opens around months 52–58 after its own build (Chapter 12). This discipline costs perhaps a year against an aggressive timeline and buys three things: credible disclosure numbers (a legal necessity in most regimes — Chapter 4), a functioning RC WORLD Academy with real classrooms (a canonical Phase 3 build item), and a flagship that has already survived the failure modes a franchisee will meet.

### 1.4 Franchise versus owned expansion — the decision framework

Franchising is the default growth mode, not the only one. The board should apply this rule set per opportunity:

- **Own** when the market is the flagship's home region (support costs near zero, brand risk highest, learning value highest), when a strategic site becomes available at exceptional terms, or when a format experiment (e.g., the first indoor arena) needs full control to iterate.
- **Franchise (single-unit or area development)** when the market is proven analogous to the flagship's, a qualified operator exists, and the support organization can service the geography (Chapter 11).
- **Master franchise** only for distant, regulated, or culturally distinct territories where a capable local partner adds more than the ~50% royalty share they cost (Chapter 3.4), and never before the domestic pilot has operated for at least a year.

> **Investor Note.** The franchise program converts RC WORLD from a single-asset leisure operator into a system business. At maturity, each full-format franchise contributes roughly $230–250 k per year to the franchisor in royalties, technology fees, and procurement margin against a marginal support cost of $60–90 k (Chapter 5.3). The equity story investors are buying in the $2.6 M flagship raise includes this option value — but the option is only exercisable if the flagship performs, which is why the two-year proof gate is written into this volume rather than left to management discretion.

## 2. Franchise Models & Formats

### 2.1 Format philosophy

The flagship is a 4.8-hectare, four-division park in a mid-size international city. Very few franchise markets will replicate those conditions exactly: urban land is scarcer and dearer, northern climates cannot run outdoor divisions year-round, and some catchments cannot support a full park's revenue requirement. The franchise system therefore offers **three engineered formats**, each a defined subset or adaptation of the flagship specification — not improvisations. A franchisee licenses a format; deviations go through the local-adaptation process (Chapter 9.5).

All three formats share the invariant core: the Shift billing unit, Toolbox Talk induction, the Tow-Truck Retrieval Protocol, the RC WORLD License and Gears programs, RCW Node telemetry on every powered asset, the bunkered charging room, the 3:1 battery ratio, electromechanical (lead-screw) rental construction fleet with hydraulics reserved for premium supervised experiences, and RC WORLD OS as the sole operating platform.

### 2.2 Format A — Full Park (4–5 ha)

The reference format: a licensed replica of the flagship at Full Park scope. Motorsport Division (Tracks A/B/C), Construction Division with Mining and Agriculture Zones, Aviation Division (netted airfield), Marine Division (pond complex), The Works, entry pavilion, restaurant, retail, events lawn. The franchisee builds in two compressed phases (Core Park then Full Park, typically 24–30 months to full scope rather than the flagship's 30) because the design is already proven — no experimentation budget, no layout iteration.

Fleet at maturity ≈ **195 powered assets** (the flagship's ~150 Phase 1 baseline plus ~20 aircraft and ~24 vessels). Mature revenue potential is benchmarked at 85–100% of the flagship's Year 5 canon ($3.4 M), i.e., **$2.4–2.9 M by the franchise's Year 3–4 and $2.9–3.4 M at full maturity**, depending on catchment. Suits peri-urban land in cities of 1.5 M+ metro population.

### 2.3 Format B — Compact Urban (~1.5 ha)

A dense, two-division park for expensive urban and inner-suburban land: **Motorsport Division plus Construction Division only** — Tracks A and B (Track C crawler trail in a compressed 400 m² technical course), Mining Zone, a reduced Agriculture Zone (optional; default is Mining plus crawler course), The Works at 60% flagship floor area, entry pavilion with F&B kiosk and retail counter, no restaurant, no aviation, no marine. This is deliberately the flagship's proven Phase 1 "Core Park" scope, densified onto 1.2–1.8 ha.

The compact format trades breadth for footfall: an urban catchment of 1 M+ within 30 minutes supports higher utilization per asset than the flagship's peri-urban site. Fleet ≈ **115–125 powered assets** (motorsport 64, construction and mining ~30, crawlers 16, recovery 4, plus utility). Single-phase build, 9–12 months. Mature revenue potential **$1.6–1.9 M** — above the flagship's $1.28 M Year 1 (which was a ramp year at the same scope) because the format assumes a denser catchment and opens with the benefit of every lesson the flagship learned.

### 2.4 Format C — Indoor Arena (cold climates)

For markets where an outdoor season shorter than ~7 months breaks the outdoor formats' economics (Scandinavia, Canada, northern US, parts of Central Europe) — and equally viable in extreme-heat markets as a climate-controlled variant (Chapter 3.3). A leased industrial building of **6,000–9,000 m²** with 6 m+ clear height houses: an indoor asphalt/drift circuit (Track A specification, Volume 3 Chapter 10 indoor annex), an indoor off-road course on engineered soil trays, a Mining Zone under dust management, a crawler course exploiting vertical structures, The Works, charging bunker, F&B kiosk, party rooms. No aviation (ceiling and netting constraints limit it to micro/indoor classes as an optional premium module), no marine beyond an optional 100 m² shallow pool module.

Fleet ≈ **90–110 powered assets**. The format's structural advantage is **weather-independent, 12-month utilization and evening trade** (indoor lighting is cheap; the flagship needed Phase 3 night-racing lighting to unlock evenings). Its structural burdens are rent, HVAC, and dust control. Mature revenue potential **$1.2–1.6 M**.

### 2.5 Format comparison table

All monetary figures are derived proportionally from the canonical flagship baseline (Volume 10) and stated as ranges pending each site's approved business plan. Headcount is mature-state FTE, with weekend casuals excluded.

| Metric | A — Full Park | B — Compact Urban | C — Indoor Arena |
|---|---|---|---|
| Land / premises | 4–5 ha leased peri-urban | 1.2–1.8 ha urban/inner-suburban | 6,000–9,000 m² leased industrial building, ≥6 m clear |
| Divisions | Motorsport, Construction (Mining + Agriculture), Aviation, Marine | Motorsport + Construction (Mining) only | Indoor Motorsport + Construction; optional micro-aviation & pool modules |
| Build program | Two phases, 24–30 months to full scope | Single phase, 9–12 months | Single phase (fit-out), 6–9 months |
| Capex (ex-franchise fee) | $3.4–4.0 M phased | $1.3–1.6 M | $1.6–2.1 M |
| Initial franchise fee | $150,000 | $90,000 | $110,000 |
| Total cash funding requirement¹ | $2.7–3.1 M | $1.6–1.95 M | $2.0–2.45 M |
| Fleet (powered assets, mature) | ~195 | 115–125 | 90–110 |
| Batteries (3:1 doctrine) | ~585 packs | ~360 packs | ~310 packs |
| Headcount (mature FTE) | 26–34 | 14–18 | 12–16 |
| Artisans among headcount | 8–10 | 5–6 | 4–5 |
| Mature revenue potential | $2.9–3.4 M (Yr 5+) | $1.6–1.9 M (Yr 3+) | $1.2–1.6 M (Yr 3+) |
| Pre-fee EBITDA margin at maturity | 24–28% | 27–30% | 25–28% |
| Post-fee EBITDA margin at maturity | 15–18% | 17–19% | 15–18% |
| Base-case payback on cash funding | Year 6–7 | Late Year 6 | Year 6–7 |
| Seasonality exposure | High (mitigated by the all-weather upgrade, Section 2.6) | High | Minimal |
| Primary catchment requirement | ≥750 k within 45 min | ≥1 M within 30 min | ≥600 k within 30 min |

¹ Cash funding requirement = phased capex funded externally plus initial fee, pre-opening costs, and working capital; later-phase capex in Format A is partly funded from operating cash flow, mirroring the flagship's $2.6 M funding against $3.9 M total capex (Volume 10).

### 2.6 Format upgrade paths

Formats are starting points, not cages. Two upgrade paths are pre-engineered so that a successful franchisee grows inside the system rather than outside it:

- **B → A ("Compact-to-Full").** A compact urban franchisee whose unit sustains ≥85% of Format B's mature revenue band for four consecutive quarters may apply to develop a Full Park in an adjacent territory (their protected territory extends accordingly) at a reduced initial fee of $100,000, crediting their proven operating record against the standard discovery process. The compact unit continues operating — the formats serve different visit occasions and cannibalization at ≥20 km separation is expected to be minimal, to be verified with pilot data.
- **A + indoor module ("all-weather upgrade").** A Full Park franchisee in a seasonal market may add an indoor arena module (a scoped subset of Format C, typically 2,500–4,000 m²) on or adjacent to their site, mirroring the flagship's own Phase 3 indoor all-weather arena. This is treated as a design change through gates G1–G4, not a new franchise; no additional initial fee, fees continue on the enlarged revenue base.

Downgrades are not offered: a park that cannot sustain its format's economics is a support case (Chapter 10.4), not a re-scoping exercise.

> **Investor Note.** The compact urban format is the expected workhorse of the system: lowest absolute ticket, fastest build, and the densest revenue per hectare — and it licenses only the flagship's Phase 1 scope, which by franchise launch will have three-plus years of operating history. The full park is the flagship-equivalent statement piece for master franchisees; the indoor arena is the climate unlock. The pilot franchise (Chapter 12) should be a Format B unless the pilot candidate's market argues decisively otherwise.

## 3. International Expansion Strategy

### 3.1 Market prioritization framework

Markets are scored before any franchisee conversation begins, on four weighted axes plus a regulatory modifier. Scoring is maintained in RC WORLD OS as a living dataset; the table below defines the rubric.

| Axis | Weight | What is measured | Data sources (category) |
|---|---|---|---|
| RC culture depth | 30% | Hobby-grade RC penetration: club counts, track counts, hobby-shop density, RC e-commerce volume, event calendars | Hobby trade associations, marketplace data, club registries (2025–2026) |
| Disposable income | 25% | Household discretionary leisure spend; propensity to pay $15–59 per experience visit | National statistics, leisure-industry analysts |
| Land cost & availability | 20% | Achievable lease terms for 1.5–5 ha peri-urban or 6,000+ m² industrial | Local brokerage surveys |
| Climate | 15% | Outdoor operating days per year; heat/cold/monsoon profile; match to format A/B/C | Meteorological normals |
| Regulatory ease (modifier) | 10% | Franchise-law burden, foreign-ownership rules, licensing of amusement operations | Local counsel briefings — verify locally |

A market scoring below 60/100 is deferred regardless of franchisee enthusiasm. The global context supports patience: industry analysts (2025–2026) place the global RC car market between $1.5 B and $6.2 B depending on scope, growing 5.8–7.5% annually, with hobby-grade share rising — the addressable base is expanding in every priority region (Volume 2 carries the full market analysis).

### 3.2 Target region analysis

**Gulf states (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait).** Highest disposable income in the candidate set, strong motorsport culture (full-scale and RC), deep corporate-events demand, and government appetite for entertainment investment. Constraints: summer heat makes June–September outdoor operation marginal, so the indicated formats are Format C (climate-controlled arena) or Format A with an indoor arena built in phase one rather than as a later option, plus night operations as the default summer mode. Land is available but often via government-linked developers, favoring a **master franchise or area-development deal with a local entertainment group**. Foreign-ownership and commercial-agency rules vary sharply by emirate/state — verify locally. Priority: **first international wave**.

**Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, Philippines).** The deepest grassroots RC culture per dollar of income in the world — crawler and drift scenes are mass hobbies — plus low land costs and year-round warmth. Constraints: monsoon seasons demand the Volume 11 drainage standards without compromise plus covered pit lanes; price points must localize toward the bottom of the pricing governance band (Chapter 9.3); currency and royalty-repatriation mechanics need structuring. Indicated formats: A and B. Entry mode: single-unit or area development with hands-on franchisor support; master franchise only for archipelago markets (Indonesia, Philippines) where geography defeats direct support. Priority: **first international wave (Malaysia/Thailand), second wave (others)**.

**Europe (Germany, UK, Netherlands, Nordics, Poland).** Mature hobby markets with strong club infrastructure and high willingness to pay, but high labor costs, short outdoor seasons in the north, and demanding planning/permitting regimes. Indicated formats: C in the north, A/B in Iberia and southern France. EU pre-contractual disclosure rules and national franchise laws (e.g., France) apply — verify locally. Priority: **second wave**, led by an indoor-arena pilot in Germany or the Netherlands.

**North America (US, Canada).** The largest RC market and the most franchise-literate consumer base, with abundant peri-urban land in secondary metros. Constraints: the US is the most heavily regulated franchise-disclosure regime on earth (FDD under the FTC Franchise Rule plus state registration states — Chapter 4.2), liability-insurance costs are materially higher, and competition for family leisure spend is intense. Indicated formats: A in the Sun Belt, C in the north and Canada. Entry: **area development with experienced multi-unit operators**; do not enter the US before the franchise system has at least three operating units elsewhere and a US-counsel-prepared FDD. Priority: **third wave**.

### 3.3 Localization requirements

Every franchise adapts along four sanctioned dimensions; everything else is standard.

**Language.** RC WORLD OS ships with full internationalization: customer and staff apps, Toolbox Talk modules, License theory tests, signage packs, and waivers are translated and legally re-reviewed per market (Volume 13). Toolbox Talk voiceover and safety signage must be in the local language *and* English; the waiver must be in the contract language local counsel specifies — verify locally.

**Climate engineering — hot markets.** Shade sails over all spectator and driver rostrum areas; misting lines at queue points; charging-bunker ventilation upgraded (LiPo charging in 45 °C ambient requires forced airflow and tightened charge-rate limits per Volume 7 battery doctrine); track-surface temperature monitoring (tire compound shifts above ~55 °C surface); summer schedule pivots to 16:00–23:00 with night-racing lighting; battery storage air-conditioned to ≤28 °C (82 °F).

**Climate engineering — cold markets.** Format C as baseline; humidity control 40–55% RH for static and dust management; floor-level heating economics reviewed at design gate G2; entrance airlocks; winter tire compounds for any outdoor shoulder-season operation; LiPo cold-storage doctrine (packs warmed to ≥15 °C / 59 °F before charge or discharge).

**Cultural calendar.** The events and marketing calendar (Volume 9) re-anchors to local rhythms: Ramadan evening-hours mode in Gulf markets (peak trade after iftar); Lunar New Year and Songkran programming in Southeast Asia; European school-holiday matrices; local motorsport calendar tie-ins. Pricing promotions follow the local calendar within the governance bands of Chapter 9.3.

### 3.4 Entry modes

| Mode | Structure | When used | Fee mechanics (summary; detail Ch. 5) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single-unit franchise | One franchisee, one site, direct franchisor support | Domestic market and first units in supportable near markets | Standard fees per Chapter 5.1 |
| Area development | One franchisee commits to 3–5 units on a schedule in a defined territory | Proven markets, capable multi-unit operators (esp. North America, Gulf) | Standard fees per unit; development fee = 50% of each committed unit's initial fee, paid upfront, credited at signing; units forfeit if schedule missed |
| Master franchise | Local partner buys territory rights, sub-franchises, delivers first-line support | Distant/regulated/culturally distinct territories; only after domestic pilot has ≥12 months of operation | Territory fee $250 k–$1.2 M by market size; unit initial fees and royalties split 50/50 franchisor/master; master must operate ≥1 unit itself first |

> **Field Note.** Several jurisdictions regulate *who may franchise at all*: China, for example, has historically required a franchisor to have operated two directly-owned units for at least one year before franchising ("2+1 rule"), and several Gulf states route foreign franchises through commercial-agency registration with strong agent protections. These rules can dictate entry mode regardless of commercial preference — another reason the master-franchise route exists in the toolkit. Verify each market with local counsel before any negotiation.
